| --- | --- |
| **και** | and — the commonest word in the language |
| **ναι** | yes |
| **είναι** | is, are |
| **the mediopassive verb endings** | **-μαι, -σαι, -ται, -νται** — είμαι, κάθομαι, γράφεται |
| **a set of stems** | παιδί, γυναίκα, αίμα, αίθουσα, καινούργιος, παίζω, παίρνω, φαίνομαι, χαίρομαι, λαιμός, ναύτης? no — ναι-words only |

**The mediopassive endings are the big grammatical case.** Every verb in the middle or passive voice — **είμαι, έρχομαι, κάθομαι, θυμάμαι, φαίνομαι, χαίρομαι** — ends in **-μαι** and never **-με**. That is stage 4's grammar and this is its spelling: if a verb's *I* form ends in the *me* sound, it is **-μαι**.

**Against which, -με is the active first person plural**: **γράφουμε, θέλουμε, είμαστε**. So **-ουμε** with ε, and **-ομαι** with αι, and the two are never confused once you know which voice you are in.

**The plural endings are all ε**: **-ες** (οι γυναίκες, οι μαθητές), **-ετε** (γράφετε), **-ες** on adjectives (καλές).

**The stems have to be learned**, and the English-cousin trick works here too: **παιδί** → *paediatric*, so **αι**. **Αίμα** → *haemoglobin*, so **αι**. **Καινούργιος** → *Cenozoic*, **καινο-** meaning new. **Γυναίκα** → *gynaecology*. Four words, four English words that preserve the spelling.

**ε in stems, for contrast**: **μέρα, πέντε, δέκα, θέλω, ξέρω, μένω, φέρνω, έχω, λέω, νερό, μεγάλος**. All of them common, all of them plain **ε**.

**The one pair worth drilling as a pair**: **παιδιά** (children) and **πεδιά** (plains). Different words, different spellings, same sound — and the first is the one you will write.

**Practice.** Drill these twenty: **και, ναι, είναι, παιδί, γυναίκα, αίμα, παίζω, παίρνω, χαίρομαι, έρχομαι, μέρα, πέντε, θέλω, ξέρω, νερό, γράφουμε, γράφετε, καλές, μαθητές, μένω**. Then write the six mediopassive endings from memory.
The o sounds: ο and ω:
Two spellings, one sound, and this is the easiest of the three — because the grammar decides almost all of it.

**Where grammar decides:**

| Ending | Spelling | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| verb, 1st person singular | **-ω** | γράφω, θέλω, μπορώ, αγαπώ |
| neuter noun, singular | **-ο** | το βιβλίο, το δώρο, το πρόσωπο |
| masculine noun, nominative | **-ος** | ο δάσκαλος, ο φίλος |
| masculine noun, accusative | **-ο** | τον δάσκαλο, τον φίλο |
| adjective, neuter | **-ο** | καλό, μεγάλο |
| genitive plural | **-ων** | των παιδιών, των γυναικών |
| adverbs from adjectives | **-ως** sometimes | κυρίως, ακριβώς, τελείως |

**So: verbs take ω, nouns take ο.** That single sentence settles the overwhelming majority of cases, and it is worth saying out loud a few times because it is the most useful spelling rule in the language.

- **γράφω** — I write, with ω · **το γράψιμο** — the writing, with ο
- **θέλω** — I want · **το θέλημα** — the will

**The genitive plural -ων** is the other grammatical **ω**, and it is everywhere once stage 3 opens: **των ανθρώπων, των παιδιών, των πόλεων**.

**Where the stem has to be memorised:**

- **ω in stems**: ώρα, ωραίος, ζώο, φως, χώρα, σώμα, όνειρο? no — **ώ** words: ώρα, ωραίος, ώμος, ζώνη, χώρος, πρώτος, κώδικας, μεγάλωσα
- **ο in stems**: όνομα, όχι, πόλη, μόνο, κόσμος, δρόμος, λόγος, πρόσωπο, σπορ

**The English-cousin trick again**: **ώρα** → *hour*, from the same root; **ζώο** → *zoo*; **φως/φωτο-** → *photograph*; **χώρα** → no cousin; **πρώτος** → *prototype*; **κώδικας** → *code*. English's *o* and *oo* spellings do not map reliably, but the learned words — *photo-, proto-, zoo-, -tomy* — do preserve the ancient **ω** where it was there.

**The -ώνω verb family** is a useful cluster: **μεγαλώνω** (grow), **τελειώνω** (finish), **σηκώνω** (lift), **αρχίζω**? no. The **-ώνω** verbs all take ω in both syllables and there are dozens of them.

**One pair to drill**, because the words are common and the difference is only spelling: **μόνο** (only) and **μονό** (single) and **μόνος** (alone). Same for **καλό** (good, neuter) and **καλώ** (I call).

**Practice.** Say the rule aloud — verbs ω, nouns ο — five times. Then drill these twenty: **γράφω, θέλω, μπορώ, βιβλίο, δώρο, δάσκαλος, φίλο, καλό, ώρα, ωραίος, ζώο, φως, χώρα, όνομα, όχι, κόσμος, δρόμος, πρώτος, τελειώνω, των παιδιών**.
The endings, drilled:
The consolidation lesson of this module: every ending from stage 2 with its spelling, as one page to drill against.

**Nouns:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Masculine** | **-ος**, **-ας**, **-ης** → acc. **-ο**, **-α**, **-η** | **-οι**, **-ες**, **-ες** → acc. **-ους**, **-ες**, **-ες** |
| **Feminine** | **-α**, **-η** (unchanged in acc.) | **-ες**, or **-εις** for the **-ση/-ξη/-ψη** nouns |
| **Neuter** | **-ο**, **-ι**, **-μα** | **-α**, **-ια**, **-ματα** |

**Adjectives**: **-ος / -η / -ο**, plural **-οι / -ες / -α**, masculine accusative plural **-ους**.

**Verbs, present tense:**

| | Class A | Class B1 | Class B2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | **-ω** | **-άω / -ώ** | **-ώ** |
| you | **-εις** | **-άς** | **-είς** |
| he/she/it | **-ει** | **-άει / -ά** | **-εί** |
| we | **-ουμε** | **-άμε / -ούμε** | **-ούμε** |
| you (pl.) | **-ετε** | **-άτε** | **-είτε** |
| they | **-ουν** | **-άνε / -ούν** | **-ούν** |

**The three rules that cover nearly all of it:**

1. **A verb's *I* ends in -ω. A noun's neuter singular ends in -ο.**
2. **-ει is a verb, -η is a feminine noun, -οι is a masculine plural, -ι is a neuter.**
3. **-ες is a plural, -αι is a mediopassive verb ending.**

**Now the drill, and this is the one to repeat weekly.** Here are twenty-four forms. Read them aloud, cover them, write them from memory with accents, check, and rewrite only the wrong ones:

**γράφω · γράφεις · γράφει · γράφουμε · γράφετε · γράφουν · μπορώ · μπορείς · μπορεί · μπορούμε · αγαπάω · αγαπάς · η πόλη · οι πόλεις · η αδελφή · οι αδελφές · ο δάσκαλος · οι δάσκαλοι · τους δασκάλους · το παιδί · τα παιδιά · το μάθημα · τα μαθήματα · είμαι**

**Then the harder version**: have the English in front of you and write the Greek. *I write · you write · he writes · we write · I can · you can · the city · the cities · the teacher · the teachers · the child · the children · the lesson · the lessons · I am.*

**Where your errors will cluster**, going by what English speakers get wrong: **-ουμε** written **-ουμαι**; **-ει** and **-η** swapped; **-οι** written **-ι** in masculine plurals; **-εις** forgotten in the **-ση** plurals; and the accent dropped from **γράφουμε**.

**Practice.** Do the twenty-four-form drill now, then the English-to-Greek version tomorrow. Keep the list; it is the weekly test for this whole module.
Final -ν: when to write it:
A small rule with a lot of traffic, because the words it applies to are among the commonest in the language.

**The words that may or may not keep a final -ν:**

- **τον** and **την** — the accusative singular articles
- **έναν** — the masculine accusative of *one, a*
- **δεν** — not · **μην** — do not
- **αυτήν**, **σαν**, **πριν** — and a few others

**The rule: keep the -ν before a vowel, and before κ, π, τ, μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ, ξ, ψ. Drop it before everything else** — that is, before β, γ, δ, ζ, θ, λ, μ, ν, ρ, σ, φ, χ.

| Keep it | Drop it |
| --- | --- |
| **τον άντρα** | **το δάσκαλο** |
| **την Κυριακή** | **τη μητέρα** |
| **τον πατέρα** | **τη Θεσσαλονίκη** |
| **την τάξη** | **τη γυναίκα** |
| **έναν καφέ** | **ένα βιβλίο** (neuter anyway) |
| **στην Αθήνα** | **στη Λάρισα** |

**Why the rule is shaped like that.** The kept **-ν** is the one you can hear: before those consonants it voices them — *τον πατέρα* comes out *tom-batéra*, *την Κυριακή* as *tiŋ-gyriakí*. Before the others it would be inaudible, so the spelling drops it.

**The masculine τον keeps its -ν much more often in practice**, because dropping it would make it identical to the neuter **το** and lose the gender. Many writers and the school grammar keep **τον** always for exactly that reason, and that is the safer habit.

**δεν and μην are usually written with the -ν always**, again to avoid confusion — **δε** also exists as an old word for *but*, and **μη** as a prefix. Keeping them full is standard practice and never wrong.

**So the practical version for you:**

1. **Always write δεν and μην.**
2. **Always write τον** for the masculine.
3. **Apply the rule to την and στην**, which is where it genuinely varies.
4. **Write έναν** before a vowel or those consonants, **ένα** otherwise.

**Where it matters most: στη and στην**, which you will write in every third sentence. **στην Αθήνα, στην εκκλησία, στην τάξη** — kept; **στη Θεσσαλονίκη, στη δουλειά, στη μητέρα** — dropped.

**What the genitive plural does**: **-ων** always keeps its **ν**, in every word, with no rule to apply — **των παιδιών, των ανθρώπων**.

**Practice.** Write these twelve with the right form of the article: *(the) άντρα, μητέρα, Κυριακή, δουλειά, τάξη, γυναίκα, πατέρα, φίλο, εκκλησία, Θεσσαλονίκη, καφέ, βιβλίο*. Then write five sentences with **στη / στην** and check each one against the rule.
The accent rules in full:
Everything about the written accent, in one place, as rules to apply rather than facts to recall.

**The basics, from stage 1:**

1. **Every word of two or more syllables takes exactly one accent.**
2. **It falls on one of the last three syllables** — the rule of limitation.
3. **Monosyllables take none**, with the exceptions below.
4. **All-capital text takes none.**

**The accented monosyllables**, and the list is short and closed:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ή** | or — to distinguish it from **η**, the feminine article |
| **πού** | where? — against **που**, *that / who* |
| **πώς** | how? — against **πως**, *that* |

**And the disambiguating accent on weak pronouns.** When a weak pronoun follows a word stressed on its third-from-last syllable and could be read as a possessive, it takes an accent of its own:

- **Ο πατέρας μού είπε…** — my father **told me**… (*μού* is *to me*, not *my*)
- **Ο δάσκαλός μου** — **my** teacher (the noun takes the second accent instead)

**That is the second accent**, and the rule is the rule of limitation doing its work: adding a clitic pushes the original stress past the third syllable from the end, so a second accent appears within the limit.

- **το όνομα** → **το όνομά μου** · **ο δάσκαλος** → **ο δάσκαλός μου** · **δώσε μου το** → **δώσε μού το**

**Where the accent moves when a word inflects**, which is the part to drill:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο άνθρωπος** → **του ανθρώπου**, **τους ανθρώπους** | forward one, by the rule of limitation |
| **το μάθημα** → **του μαθήματος** | forward one |
| **η κυβέρνηση** → **οι κυβερνήσεις** | forward one |
| **ο φίλος** → **του φίλου**, **τους φίλους** | no movement — already inside the limit |

**On a digraph, the accent goes on the second letter**: **παίζω, είμαι, πού, μπορείς**.

**With a diaeresis, both marks appear** when the vowel needs separating and carries the stress: **πρωτεΐνη**, **Μαΐου**, **ταΐζω**.

**In compounds, the accent is on the second element**, usually, and the first loses its own: **πολύ + κατοικία** → **πολυκατοικία**.

**What the accent never does:** mark length, mark pitch, or distinguish anything other than stress. One mark, one job — which is why the monotonic system replaced the old three accents and two breathings in 1982.

**Practice.** Accent these ten words from memory, out loud and then written: *ανθρωπος, μαθημα, μαθηματος, δασκαλος, δασκαλου, κυβερνησεις, παιζω, ειμαι, πολυκατοικια, ονομα μου*. Then write five sentences containing a possessive and check the second accent in each.
Diaeresis, apostrophe and syllables:
Three small orthographic systems, each of which decides how a word is read, and all three are rule-based rather than memorised.

**The diaeresis — τα διαλυτικά — breaks a digraph.** Two dots over ι or υ say "read these two vowels separately":

- **παϊδάκια** — *pa-i-dákia*, lamb chops. Without the dots, **παιδάκια**, *little children*. Two different words.
- **προϊόν** — product · **γαϊδούρι** — donkey · **ευνοϊκός** — favourable

**When it is omitted — and this is the rule:** when the **first** of the two vowels carries the accent, the accent already breaks the pair, so no dots are needed.

- **Μάιος** — May · **νεράιδα** — fairy · **ρολόι** — watch · **πλάι** — beside

**When both marks appear**: when the ι or υ itself is stressed and still needs separating.

- **Μαΐου** — of May · **πρωτεΐνη** — protein · **ταΐζω** — I feed

**And it is unnecessary where there was no digraph to break**: **πρωί** (morning), **Μωυσής** (Moses), **διυλιστήριο** (refinery) — **ωι**, **ωυ** and **ιυ** are not digraphs, so nothing has to be said.

**In all capitals the dots stay**, because there are no accents to do the job: **ΠΑΪΔΑΚΙΑ**, **ΠΡΟΪΟΝ**.

**The apostrophe marks a dropped vowel** — elision — and it is everywhere in speech and writing both:

- **σ' αγαπώ** ← σε αγαπώ · **απ' την Αθήνα** ← από την Αθήνα · **μ' αρέσει** ← μου αρέσει
- **θα 'ρθω** ← θα έρθω · **να 'ναι** ← να είναι

**Which is why a word can be unfindable in a dictionary**: put the vowel back and look again.

**Syllables — ο συλλαβισμός — matter for two reasons**: hyphenating at the end of a line, and knowing which syllable the accent is on. The rules:

1. **One consonant between two vowels goes with the following vowel**: πα-τέ-ρας, μη-τέ-ρα.
2. **Two consonants between vowels go with the following vowel if a Greek word can begin with that pair**: έ-θνος, κρύ-βω, Α-φρι-κή. If not, they split: άν-θρω-πος, θάλασ-σα? — no: **θά-λασ-σα**, because *σσ* cannot begin a word.
3. **Three consonants go with the following vowel if the first two can begin a word**: αι-σχρός; otherwise the first stays behind: άν-θρω-πος.
4. **Digraphs are never split** — neither vowel pairs (αι, ει, οι, ου, αυ, ευ) nor consonant pairs (μπ, ντ, γκ, τσ, τζ).

**Counting syllables is what the accent rules need**, so this is not an idle skill: to know whether the stress is on the third from the end you have to divide the word, and digraphs count as one.

**Practice.** Add the diaeresis where it belongs: *παιδακια (chops), προιον, Μαιος, Μαιου, πρωτεινη, ρολοι*. Then expand these: **σ' αγαπώ, απ' το σπίτι, θα 'ρθω**. Then divide into syllables and say where the stress is: **άνθρωπος, θάλασσα, οικογένεια, μπορείτε, εκκλησία**.
The genitive: what it is for:
The third case, and the one that does the most jobs. Stage 2 gave you the subject and the object; this is everything else a noun can be.

**The core meaning is *of*.**

- **το σπίτι του πατέρα** — the house of the father, my father's house
- **η πόρτα του σπιτιού** — the door of the house
- **ο γιος της Μαρίας** — Maria's son

**Greek has no apostrophe-s.** Every English possessive becomes a genitive, with the owner **after** the thing owned: *the teacher's book* is **το βιβλίο του δασκάλου**, literally *the book of the teacher*.

**The seven jobs of the genitive**, which is why it is worth a whole stage:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Possession** | το σπίτι του πατέρα |
| **Of, in every sense** | το τέλος της μέρας — the end of the day |
| **The indirect object, with pronouns** | **μου** λέει — he tells **me** |
| **Dates** | στις 14 **Οκτωβρίου** |
| **Age and duration** | είμαι τριάντα **χρονών** |
| **Set time phrases** | **του χρόνου** (next year), **της Κυριακής** (Sunday's) |
| **After a few prepositions and adverbs**, mostly formal | **εναντίον** του, **λόγω** της βροχής |

**You have already been using it.** The possessives from stage 2 — **μου, σου, του, της, μας, σας, τους** — are the weak genitive pronouns. **Ο φίλος μου** is *the friend of me*. So the case is not new; what is new is doing it with full nouns.

**What the genitive is *not* used for in Modern Greek**, and this matters because the older language did use it:

- **Not after most prepositions.** Those take the accusative: **για τον φίλο μου**, not *για του φίλου*.
- **Not as the indirect object with a full noun.** *I give the book to George* is **Δίνω το βιβλίο στον Γιώργο** — **σε** plus the accusative, not a genitive. Only the pronouns use the genitive there.
- **Not with most verbs.** Ancient Greek had verbs taking the genitive; the modern language has very few.

**So the genitive has shrunk**, which is good news, and what is left is concentrated: *of*, possession, pronouns as indirect objects, dates and a handful of fixed phrases.

**The genitive plural is the one form everybody avoids.** It exists, it is regular, and Greeks themselves sometimes rephrase to dodge it — **των κυβερνήσεων** is a mouthful. It has its own lesson and it is worth learning properly rather than avoiding.

**Practice.** Say these aloud and notice the shape — *thing owned, then owner in the genitive*: **το σπίτι του πατέρα · το βιβλίο του δασκάλου · ο γιος της Μαρίας · η πόρτα του σπιτιού**. Then say *my mother's house* and *the child's name* out loud, in Greek, and check the order.
The genitive of the article:
The twelve-cell article table is now complete, and this is the row to learn cold.

**The genitive forms:**

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Singular** | του | της | του |
| **Plural** | των | των | των |

**And the whole table, finally, in one place:**

| | Masc. sg. | Fem. sg. | Neut. sg. | Masc. pl. | Fem. pl. | Neut. pl. |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | ο | η | το | οι | οι | τα |
| **Accusative** | τον | την | το | τους | τις | τα |
| **Genitive** | του | της | του | των | των | των |

**Eighteen cells, nine distinct words**: ο, η, το, τον, την, οι, τα, τους, τις, του, της, των. Say them until they are automatic — this is the single most load-bearing memorisation in Greek grammar, as stage 2's consolidation lesson argued.

**Note the two collisions, because they cause real ambiguity:**

1. **του** is both masculine and neuter genitive singular. **Το βιβλίο του παιδιού** (the child's book) and **το βιβλίο του δασκάλου** (the teacher's) use the same article form.
2. **των** is the genitive plural for all three genders. One word for everything, which is a mercy.

**And one more collision worth flagging**: **του** and **της** are also the weak pronouns *his* and *her*. **Ο φίλος του** is *his friend*; **ο φίλος του δασκάλου** is *the teacher's friend*. Same word, different job, and position tells you which: a pronoun stands alone, an article is followed by its noun.

**The article is repeated in a genitive phrase**, and this is the structural thing to get right:

- **το σπίτι του πατέρα** — two articles, one for each noun.
- **η πόρτα του σπιτιού** — the same.
- **το όνομα της γυναίκας του αδελφού μου** — the name of the wife of my brother. Three articles, three nouns, and perfectly ordinary Greek.

**That stacking is how Greek builds what English does with apostrophes and *of***, and it goes as deep as you like without becoming unnatural.

**Practice.** Say the full eighteen-cell table aloud, down each column, five times. Then say these with both articles: *the father's house · the teacher's book · the child's name · the woman's son · the children's books*. Then say **το όνομα της γυναίκας του αδελφού μου** until it comes out in one piece.
The genitive: masculine nouns:
Three patterns, and the **-ος** one has a stress shift that catches everyone.

**ο δάσκαλος:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | ο δάσκαλος | οι δάσκαλοι |
| **Accusative** | τον δάσκαλο | τους δασκάλους |
| **Genitive** | **του δασκάλου** | **των δασκάλων** |

**ο πατέρας:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Genitive** | **του πατέρα** | **των πατέρων** |

**ο μαθητής:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Genitive** | **του μαθητή** | **των μαθητών** |

**The three rules:**

1. **-ος** nouns take **-ου** in the genitive singular and **-ων** in the plural.
2. **-ας** and **-ης** nouns take **the bare stem** in the genitive singular — the same as the accusative — and **-ων** in the plural.
3. **The genitive plural is -ων for every masculine noun.** No exceptions worth learning.

**The stress moves, and this is the part to drill.** In **-ος** nouns stressed on the third syllable from the end, the genitive forces it forward:

- **ο άνθρωπος** → **του ανθρώπου**, **των ανθρώπων**
- **ο δάσκαλος** → **του δασκάλου**, **των δασκάλων**
- **ο ουρανός** → **του ουρανού** — already on the ending, so nothing moves

**In -ης nouns the plural stress goes to the ending**: **ο μαθητής** → **των μαθητών**; **ο εργάτης** → **των εργατών**.

**So the genitive is where the rule of limitation earns its keep.** A noun's genitive is predictable from its nominative plus that rule, which means you are applying a rule rather than memorising four forms per word.

**The useful examples, in phrases you will actually say:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο γιος του παπά** | the priest's son |
| **το σπίτι του πατέρα μου** | my father's house |
| **το όνομα του αδελφού σου** | your brother's name |
| **η γυναίκα του δασκάλου** | the teacher's wife |
| **τα παιδιά των γειτόνων** | the neighbours' children |

**Note ο παπάς → του παπά**, which belongs to the **-ας** pattern despite looking unusual.

**Practice.** Give all six forms of **ο φίλος**, **ο άντρας** and **ο μαθητής**, out loud. Then say: *the teacher's book · my father's house · the priest's son · the children of the neighbours*. Then do **ο άνθρωπος** in all six and check where the stress sits in each.
The genitive: feminine nouns:
The feminines were the easy gender for two cases and they are the awkward one here — because the genitive is the only place where they change.

**η γυναίκα:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nominative** | η γυναίκα | οι γυναίκες |
| **Accusative** | την γυναίκα | τις γυναίκες |
| **Genitive** | **της γυναίκας** | **των γυναικών** |

**η αδελφή:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Genitive** | **της αδελφής** | **των αδελφών** |

**η πόλη:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Genitive** | **της πόλης** | **των πόλεων** |

**The rules:**

1. **Genitive singular adds -ς**: γυναίκα → γυναίκας, αδελφή → αδελφής, πόλη → πόλης.
2. **Genitive plural is -ων**, with the stress on it: γυναικών, αδελφών.
3. **The -ση/-ξη/-ψη nouns take -εων** in the genitive plural: **των πόλεων**, **των τάξεων**, **των κυβερνήσεων** — and the stress moves to the **-ε-**.

**That third rule produces the forms Greeks themselves find heavy**, and the reason is visible: these are ancient third-declension nouns carrying an ancient ending. **Των κυβερνήσεων** is correct, formal and a mouthful; in speech people often restructure the sentence to avoid it. Learn it anyway — it is all over written Greek.

**The stress in the genitive singular does not move**: **της γυναίκας**, **της θάλασσας**, **της κυβέρνησης**. Only the plural moves.

**The -ος feminines**, from stage 2: **η οδός** → **της οδού**, **των οδών**. They follow the masculine **-ος** pattern with feminine articles, and **οδός** is on every street sign: **οδός Ερμού** — *Ermou Street*, with **Ερμού** itself a genitive.

**That is worth noticing: Greek street names are genitives.** **Οδός Σταδίου**, **Λεωφόρος Αλεξάνδρας**, **Πλατεία Συντάγματος** — *the street of the Stadium*, *the avenue of Alexandra*, *the square of the Constitution*. Once you see it, every street sign in Greece becomes a genitive exercise.

**Church examples**, since they are everywhere in the same shape: **η εορτή της Παναγίας** (the feast of the Mother of God), **η Κυριακή της Ορθοδοξίας** (the Sunday of Orthodoxy), **ο ναός της Αγίας Σοφίας** (the church of Holy Wisdom).

**Practice.** Give all six forms of **η μέρα**, **η φίλη** and **η τάξη**. Then say: *the woman's name · my sister's house · the door of the city · the feast of the Mother of God*. Then read three Greek street names aloud and say what each genitive means.
The genitive: neuter nouns:
The neuters change in the genitive too — and the **-μα** nouns do something that explains their plural at the same time.

**το βιβλίο:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom./acc.** | το βιβλίο | τα βιβλία |
| **Genitive** | **του βιβλίου** | **των βιβλίων** |

**το παιδί:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom./acc.** | το παιδί | τα παιδιά |
| **Genitive** | **του παιδιού** | **των παιδιών** |

**το μάθημα:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom./acc.** | το μάθημα | τα μαθήματα |
| **Genitive** | **του μαθήματος** | **των μαθημάτων** |

**The rules:**

1. **-ο** nouns: genitive **-ου**, plural **-ων**.
2. **-ι** nouns: genitive **-ιού** with the stress on the ending, plural **-ιών**.
3. **-μα** nouns: genitive **-ματος**, plural **-μάτων**. The **-ματ-** that appears in the plural is the real stem, and the genitive shows why: these are third-declension nouns whose stem ends in **-ματ-** and whose nominative dropped the **-τ**.

**Which means το μάθημα is really μαθηματ-**, and English has the evidence: *mathematics*, *dogmatic*, *problematic*, *thematic*, *schematic*. Every English **-mat-** word is this Greek stem showing through.

**The stress in -ι genitives always goes to the ending**: **του παιδιού**, **του σπιτιού**, **του ψωμιού**, **του κρασιού**. That is regular and worth saying aloud a few times, because it feels wrong at first.

**The -ος neuters** — **το δάσος**, **το μέρος**, **το έθνος** — take **-ους** in the genitive singular and **-ων** in the plural: **του δάσους**, **των δασών**. They have their own lesson later in this stage.

**Phrases in use:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **η πόρτα του σπιτιού** | the door of the house |
| **το όνομα του παιδιού** | the child's name |
| **το τέλος του μαθήματος** | the end of the lesson |
| **τα παιχνίδια των παιδιών** | the children's toys |
| **η μέρα του Αγίου Γεωργίου** | St George's day |

**Practice.** Give all four forms of **το δώρο**, **το σπίτι** and **το όνομα**. Then say: *the door of the house · the child's name · the end of the lesson · the children's books*. Then say **του παιδιού, του σπιτιού, του ψωμιού, του κρασιού** five times, with the stress on the ending.
The genitive plural:
One ending, **-ων**, for every noun in the language — and the form that Greeks themselves sometimes avoid. Worth a lesson of its own because it is where the stress rules all arrive at once.

**The ending is -ων**, always, with these shapes:

| Pattern | Genitive plural |
| --- | --- |
| ο δάσκαλος | των δασκάλων |
| ο πατέρας | των πατέρων |
| ο μαθητής | των μαθητών |
| η γυναίκα | των γυναικών |
| η αδελφή | των αδελφών |
| η πόλη | **των πόλεων** |
| το βιβλίο | των βιβλίων |
| το παιδί | των παιδιών |
| το μάθημα | των μαθημάτων |

**The article is των for all three genders**, so the only question is the noun's ending — and that is **-ων** in every row, with **-εων** for the **-ση/-ξη/-ψη** feminines.

**Where the stress goes**, and this is the whole difficulty:

1. **Masculine -ος**: on the ending's own syllable if the rule of limitation requires it — **των ανθρώπων** (third from end, legal), **των δασκάλων**.
2. **Masculine -ης, feminines in -α and -η**: on the ending — **των μαθητών, των γυναικών, των αδελφών**.
3. **-ι neuters**: on the ending — **των παιδιών, των σπιτιών**.
4. **-μα neuters**: third from the end — **των μαθημάτων, των ονομάτων**.
5. **-εων feminines**: on the **-ε-** — **των πόλεων, των τάξεων**.

**Why Greeks avoid some of them.** **Των κυβερνήσεων**, **των συνεντεύξεων**, **των ανακαινίσεων** are heavy, and spoken Greek often restructures: **τα παιδιά των γειτόνων** stays, but a long **-εων** form gets turned into a **σε** phrase or a different sentence. You will hear the avoidance; do not copy it until you can produce the form you are avoiding.

**Where the genitive plural is unavoidable:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **τα δικαιώματα των ανθρώπων** | human rights |
| **η γλώσσα των παιδιών** | the children's language |
| **ο κόσμος των βιβλίων** | the world of books |
| **η ιστορία των Ελλήνων** | the history of the Greeks |
| **η Κυριακή των Βαΐων** | Palm Sunday — *the Sunday of the palms* |
| **η εορτή των Αγίων Πάντων** | All Saints |

**The last two are church Greek in the modern language**, and the pattern — a feast named with a genitive plural — is everywhere in the calendar.

**Practice.** Say the nine-row table aloud twice. Then give the genitive plural of: **ο φίλος, ο άντρας, η μέρα, η πόλη, το παιδί, το όνομα, η τάξη**. Then say the six phrases, and **των κυβερνήσεων** three times without flinching.
Possession: the two ways:
Greek has two ways of saying whose something is, and they are not interchangeable. This lesson is when to use which.

**Way one: the weak pronoun, from stage 2.** For people — *my, your, his, her, our, their*:

- **ο φίλος μου** — my friend · **το σπίτι τους** — their house

**Way two: the genitive of a full noun.** For anything named:

- **το σπίτι του πατέρα** — my father's house · **η πόρτα του σπιτιού** — the door of the house

**So the rule is simple: pronoun for a pronoun, genitive for a noun.** You cannot say *το σπίτι του* meaning *the father's house* without naming the father, and you would not say *το σπίτι του πατέρα μου μου* — the two do not stack on the same noun.

**But they combine across nouns**, and this is how real Greek sentences are built:

- **το σπίτι του πατέρα μου** — the house of my father. **μου** attaches to **πατέρα**, and **πατέρα** is in the genitive because of **σπίτι**.
- **το όνομα της γυναίκας του αδελφού μου** — the name of my brother's wife.

**Read those from the right.** *My brother* → *my brother's wife* → *the name of my brother's wife*. The chain builds outward and each link is a genitive.

**The emphatic form: δικός μου.** When the possession is the point — *mine*, *my own* — Greek uses an adjective:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αυτό είναι δικό μου.** | This is mine. |
| **Είναι δικό σου;** | Is it yours? |
| **το δικό μου σπίτι** | my own house |
| **ο δικός της άντρας** | her own husband |

**δικός inflects like an adjective** and agrees with the thing owned, while the pronoun after it says the owner: **δικός μου** (masc.), **δική μου** (fem.), **δικό μου** (neut.), **δικοί μου** (masc. pl.).

**For asking whose: ποιανού.**

- **Ποιανού είναι αυτό;** — Whose is this?
- **Ποιανού παιδιού;** — Which child's?

**And the social use worth knowing.** In a Greek parish people are identified by genitive: **ο γιος του παπά**, **η κόρη της Μαρίας**, **η γυναίκα του Γιώργου**, **τα παιδιά του Νίκου**. Naming someone by whose they are is normal, warm and the usual way of placing a person — and it means the genitive is not a grammar exercise but the way you will be talked about.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **ο φίλος μου · το σπίτι του πατέρα μου · το όνομα της γυναίκας του αδελφού μου · Αυτό είναι δικό μου · Ποιανού είναι;** Then describe four people in your parish by genitive — *whose son, whose wife, whose daughter* — out loud.
Names in the genitive:
Greek names decline like any other noun, and the genitive of a name is something you will need constantly — for saying whose, for dates, and for street signs.

**Men's names, by ending:**

| Nominative | Genitive | Vocative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ο Γιώργος | του Γιώργου | Γιώργο! |
| ο Νίκος | του Νίκου | Νίκο! |
| ο Κωνσταντίνος | του Κωνσταντίνου | Κωνσταντίνε! |
| ο Γιάννης | του Γιάννη | Γιάννη! |
| ο Μανώλης | του Μανώλη | Μανώλη! |
| ο Δημήτρης | του Δημήτρη | Δημήτρη! |
| ο Ανδρέας | του Ανδρέα | Ανδρέα! |

**Women's names:**

| Nominative | Genitive |
| --- | --- |
| η Μαρία | της Μαρίας |
| η Ελένη | της Ελένης |
| η Άννα | της Άννας |
| η Σοφία | της Σοφίας |
| η Δέσποινα | της Δέσποινας |

**Women's names have no separate vocative** — you call someone by the nominative: **Μαρία!**

**Surnames are genitives already**, very often: **Παπαδόπουλος** means *son of the priest*, and family surnames in **-ου** are genitive forms — **Μαρία Παπαδοπούλου** is *Maria [daughter] of Papadopoulos*. Which is why a woman's surname differs from her father's or husband's by one ending:

- **Γιώργος Παπαδόπουλος** → **Μαρία Παπαδοπούλου**
- **Νίκος Βασιλείου** → **Ελένη Βασιλείου** (already genitive, so unchanged)

**That is worth knowing before you read a parish list**, because the same family appears in two spellings and both are correct.

**Saints' names in the genitive** are how the calendar is written:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **του Αγίου Γεωργίου** | of St George — 23 April |
| **της Αγίας Παρασκευής** | of St Paraskevi |
| **του Αγίου Νικολάου** | of St Nicholas |
| **των Αγίων Κωνσταντίνου και Ελένης** | of SS Constantine and Helen |

**And name days are said with the genitive**: **Γιορτάζει του Αγίου Γεωργίου** — *he celebrates on St George's day*. If someone in the parish is named Γιώργος, 23 April is his day and **Χρόνια πολλά** is what you say.

**Addressing someone by name: use the vocative.** **Γιώργο, τι κάνεις;** — not *Γιώργος*. Using the nominative to call someone is a small, audible error, and the vocative is the form you will say more than any other, so it is worth getting automatic.

**Practice.** Say the genitive and vocative of five names you know from your parish. Then say: *the son of George · the daughter of Maria · St Nicholas's day*. Then call five people by name, out loud, in the vocative.
Dates:
How Greek writes and says a date — which needs the genitive of the month and the ordinal numbers.

**The pattern: the number, then the month in the genitive.**

- **14 Οκτωβρίου** — the 14th of October
- **25 Μαρτίου** — the 25th of March
- **1 Μαΐου** — the 1st of May (and note **Μαΐου** with both marks, from the Spelling track)

**The months in the genitive:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ιανουαρίου | of January | Ιουλίου | of July |
| Φεβρουαρίου | of February | Αυγούστου | of August |
| Μαρτίου | of March | Σεπτεμβρίου | of September |
| Απριλίου | of April | Οκτωβρίου | of October |
| Μαΐου | of May | Νοεμβρίου | of November |
| Ιουνίου | of June | Δεκεμβρίου | of December |

**Saying the day: the neuter ordinal**, because the understood noun is **ημέρα**? — no, it is the number itself used as a noun, and Greek uses the plain cardinal in speech for most days:

- **σήμερα είναι 14 Οκτωβρίου** — said *δεκατέσσερις Οκτωβρίου*, with the feminine form of 4, because the understood word is the feminine **ημέρα**.
- **Την πρώτη Μαΐου** — on the first of May, using the ordinal **πρώτη**, feminine.

**The first of the month takes the ordinal**: **η πρώτη** (**την πρώτη Ιανουαρίου**). Every other day takes the cardinal.

**On a date: στις.**

- **στις 14 Οκτωβρίου** — on 14 October
- **στις 25 Δεκεμβρίου** — on 25 December
- **την 1η Μαΐου** — on 1 May

**The year** is said as a number, with **το** : **το 2026** — *το δύο χιλιάδες είκοσι έξι*. In full: **στις 14 Οκτωβρίου 2026**.

**The written forms:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **14/10/2026** | day first, as in Britain |
| **14 Οκτωβρίου 2026** | the full form |
| **14.10.26** | informal |

**Asking:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι μέρα είναι σήμερα;** | What day is it today? |
| **Πόσες του μηνός έχουμε;** | What is the date? (*how many of the month do we have* — and **του μηνός** is an old genitive) |
| **Πότε είναι;** | When is it? |

**The church calendar is written this way everywhere** — a notice board gives the feast and the date in exactly this shape: **Κυριακή 26 Οκτωβρίου — Αγίου Δημητρίου**. Reading those two lines is a date, a genitive and a saint's name, all of which you now have.

**One historical note worth having.** Greece uses the Gregorian calendar for civil dates; the Church in Greece uses the New Calendar for fixed feasts and the old reckoning for Pascha, which is why Greek Easter usually falls on a different Sunday from the Western one. The dates on the notice board are the Church's.

**Practice.** Say today's date aloud, in full. Then say your own birthday, and the dates of three feasts you know. Then read the next four entries off a church notice board and say each one.
Age, and how long things last:
Two small systems that both use the genitive, and both come up in the first conversation you have with anyone.

**Age: the genitive plural of χρόνος.**

- **Είμαι τριάντα χρονών.** — I am thirty.
- **Πόσων χρονών είσαι;** — How old are you?
- **Το παιδί είναι πέντε χρονών.** — The child is five.

**χρονών is a genitive plural** — *of years* — and it is irregular enough to learn as a word: **ο χρόνος** (year, time) → **των χρόνων**, but the age form is **χρονών**. Both exist; **χρονών** is what you say about age.

**The alternative, more formal**: **ετών** — from **το έτος** (year), the learned word. **Είμαι 30 ετών** is what a form or a document says. You will read it; you need not say it.

**For children, Greeks often use the months**: **οκτώ μηνών** — eight months old.

**Duration: for how long.**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **για δύο μέρες** | for two days |
| **για μια βδομάδα** | for a week |
| **για τρεις μήνες** | for three months |
| **για ένα χρόνο** | for a year |

**για plus the accusative**, so no genitive here — the genitive is for age, and **για** keeps its ordinary case.

**How long have you been doing something: the present tense with a time phrase.**

- **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά έναν χρόνο.** — I have been learning Greek for a year. (*I learn Greek one year*)
- **Μένω εδώ πέντε χρόνια.** — I have lived here five years.

**Greek uses the present** where English uses a perfect, because the action is still going on. That is a real difference and it is worth noticing: *I have lived here five years* in Greek is *I live here five years*.

**The time words you need with it:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **η μέρα** | day | **η βδομάδα** | week |
| **ο μήνας** | month | **ο χρόνος** | year |
| **η ώρα** | hour | **το λεπτό** | minute |
| **σήμερα** | today | **αύριο** | tomorrow |
| **χθες** | yesterday | **μεθαύριο** | the day after tomorrow |
| **τώρα** | now | **μετά** | after, later |
| **πριν** | before, ago | **ακόμα** | still, yet |

**Two fixed genitive phrases** worth having, because they are extremely common and they are genitives:

- **του χρόνου** — next year
- **της Κυριακής** — Sunday's, of Sunday — as in **το κήρυγμα της Κυριακής**

**Practice.** Say your age, then the ages of three people you know. Then ask **Πόσων χρονών είσαι;** aloud. Then say: *I have been learning Greek for a year · I have lived here five years · for two days · next year*.
The indirect object:
Who something is given, said or sent to. Greek does it two ways and which one depends entirely on whether it is a pronoun or a noun.

**With a pronoun: the weak genitive.** The same **μου, σου, του, της, μας, σας, τους** as the possessives, placed before the verb:

- **Μου λέει.** — He tells me.
- **Σου δίνω το βιβλίο.** — I am giving you the book.
- **Της έγραψα.** — I wrote to her.
- **Τους μίλησα.** — I spoke to them.

**With a noun: σε plus the accusative.**

- **Δίνω το βιβλίο στον Γιώργο.** — I am giving the book to George.
- **Λέω στη μητέρα μου.** — I am telling my mother.
- **Γράφω στον αδελφό μου.** — I am writing to my brother.

**Never a genitive noun.** *Δίνω το βιβλίο του Γιώργου* means *I am giving George's book* — the genitive makes it possession, not the recipient. This is the one place where mixing the two systems changes the meaning outright, so it is worth drilling.

**Both at once, when the thing is a pronoun too**, with the indirect first:

- **Μου το δίνει.** — He gives it to me.
- **Σου το λέω.** — I am telling you it.
- **Της τα έστειλα.** — I sent them to her.

**After a command they follow the verb**, in the same order:

- **Δώσε μου το!** — Give it to me!
- **Πες μου την αλήθεια.** — Tell me the truth.

**The verbs that take an indirect object** are the ones you would expect, and they are high-frequency: **δίνω** (give), **λέω** (say, tell), **γράφω** (write), **στέλνω** (send), **δείχνω** (show), **εξηγώ** (explain), **φέρνω** (bring), **μιλάω** (speak — with **σε**: μιλάω στον Γιώργο), **απαντάω** (answer), **τηλεφωνώ** (telephone — takes the genitive pronoun: **σου τηλεφωνώ**).

**And the ones that look like they should and do not**: **ρωτάω** (ask) takes a plain accusative — **σε ρωτάω**, *I ask you* — and **βοηθάω** (help) likewise: **σε βοηθάω**.

**So three groups**, and the deck stores which is which: verbs with a genitive pronoun (**μου λέει**), verbs with an accusative pronoun (**με ρωτάει**), and verbs with **σε** plus a noun. Most are predictable from English; the exceptions are **ρωτάω** and **βοηθάω**.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **Μου λέει · Σου δίνω το βιβλίο · Της έγραψα · Δίνω το βιβλίο στον Γιώργο · Μου το δίνει · Δώσε μου το**. Then say the difference out loud between **Δίνω το βιβλίο στον Γιώργο** and **Δίνω το βιβλίο του Γιώργου**.
The vocative:
The fourth case, and the one you will use most often in a day — because it is how you speak to someone rather than about them.

**What it is.** The form of a noun used when you address the person or thing directly. English has no such form; Greek has one and using the wrong case is immediately audible.

**Masculine -ος nouns take -ε:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ο Γιώργος | **Γιώργο!** |
| ο δάσκαλος | **δάσκαλε!** |
| ο φίλος | **φίλε!** |
| ο κύριος | **κύριε!** |
| ο Κωνσταντίνος | **Κωνσταντίνε!** |

**Note that two-syllable names in -ος often take -ο rather than -ε**: **Γιώργο**, **Νίκο**, **Πέτρο** — while longer and more formal ones take **-ε**: **Κωνσταντίνε**, **Αλέξανδρε**, **δάσκαλε**. Both patterns are standard and the short one is what you will use with names.

**Masculine -ας and -ης nouns drop the -ς:**

- **ο πατέρας** → **πατέρα!** · **ο Γιάννης** → **Γιάννη!** · **ο μαθητής** → **μαθητή!** · **ο παπάς** → **παπά!**

**Feminines and neuters are the same as the nominative:**

- **η Μαρία** → **Μαρία!** · **η μητέρα** → **μητέρα!** · **το παιδί** → **παιδί!**

**The article is dropped.** **Γιώργο, τι κάνεις;** — never *ο Γιώργο*. That is the other half of the vocative: no article, ever.

**The forms you will actually use:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πάτερ!** | Father — to a priest. The old vocative of πατέρας, kept for this use. |
| **κύριε / κυρία** | sir / madam — and *Mr / Mrs* with a surname |
| **παιδιά!** | *everyone* — literally *children*, used to address a group of any age |
| **ρε!** | an untranslatable familiar particle — **ρε Γιώργο**, *oi, George*. Friends only. |
| **αγάπη μου** | my love · **παιδί μου** — my child, used affectionately to adults |
| **φίλε μου** | my friend |

**Πάτερ is a genuine survival**, like **Δόξα τω Θεώ**: the modern vocative of **πατέρας** is **πατέρα**, but the older **Πάτερ** is fixed for addressing a priest. Use it.

**ρε is worth understanding and not using early.** It marks familiarity and it can be warm or rude depending on who says it to whom. Between friends it is constant; from a stranger it is a provocation. Hear it for a year before you use it.

**Practice.** Say the vocative of ten names you know. Then say: **Γιώργο, τι κάνεις; · Πάτερ, καλημέρα. · Κύριε, συγγνώμη. · Παιδιά, πάμε!** Then call four people by name without the article, and notice how wrong *ο Γιώργο* sounds once you are listening for it.
κύριε, κυρία and how Greeks address each:
The social system around names and titles. It is simpler than the French or German version and it has one feature English does not: the first name with the title.

**The basic titles:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο κύριος** / **κύριε** | Mr, sir |
| **η κυρία** / **κυρία** | Mrs, madam |
| **η κυρία** also | Ms — there is no separate form, and **δεσποινίς** (Miss) is old-fashioned and dying |

**With the surname**, formally: **κύριε Παπαδόπουλε** — note the surname is in the vocative too.

**With the first name**, which is the distinctively Greek option: **κυρία Μαρία**, **κύριε Γιώργο**. It is polite and warm at once — respectful without being distant — and it is what you will hear most in a parish, a shop you use often, or a neighbourhood.

**That middle register has no English equivalent** and it is worth adopting: **κυρία Ελένη** to the older woman who runs the candle desk is exactly right, where *Mrs Papadopoulou* would be stiff and *Eleni* would be forward.

**For the clergy:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πάτερ** | Father — the parish priest, always |
| **πάτερ Γιώργο** | Father George — first name, as with κυρία |
| **ο παπα-Γιώργης** | the priest George — the affectionate compound you will hear in the third person |
| **Σεβασμιώτατε** | Your Eminence — a metropolitan or bishop |
| **Παναγιώτατε** | Your All-Holiness — the Ecumenical Patriarch |
| **Γέροντα** | Elder — a monastic elder or spiritual father |

**In the third person**: **ο πατέρας Γιώργος**, **ο παπάς**, **ο ιερέας**, or **ο Γέροντας**. **Παπάς** is informal and affectionate rather than disrespectful, which surprises English speakers.

**Other words of address worth knowing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **γιατρέ** | doctor — the vocative of **ο γιατρός** |
| **δάσκαλε** | teacher — also used admiringly to a master of anything |
| **κυρ-Γιώργη** / **κυρά-Μαρία** | the old rural forms, still heard, affectionate |
| **θεία** / **θείε** | aunt / uncle — used to any older person you are close to, not only relatives |
| **κουμπάρε** | the word for your child's godfather or your wedding sponsor — a close relationship, and used as a familiar greeting between men |

**θεία and θείος used of non-relatives** is worth knowing because it will be used of you eventually, and it is a compliment: it places you in the family.

**The name-day habit, again.** When you know someone's name you know their feast, and **Χρόνια πολλά** on that day is one of the most valued small courtesies in Greek life. Learning the parish's names is learning its calendar.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **κύριε Παπαδόπουλε · κυρία Μαρία · Πάτερ · πάτερ Γιώργο · γιατρέ · παιδιά**. Then decide what you would call five specific people at your church, and say each form out loud.
The full adjective table:
Adjectives in all four cases, both numbers, three genders — which is twenty-four forms and three patterns' worth of endings you already know.

**καλός — good, the commonest pattern:**

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | καλός | καλή | καλό |
| **Acc. sg.** | καλό | καλή | καλό |
| **Gen. sg.** | καλού | καλής | καλού |
| **Voc. sg.** | καλέ | καλή | καλό |
| **Nom. pl.** | καλοί | καλές | καλά |
| **Acc. pl.** | καλούς | καλές | καλά |
| **Gen. pl.** | καλών | καλών | καλών |

**It is the noun endings again** — masculine like **δάσκαλος**, feminine like **αδελφή**, neuter like **βιβλίο** — so nothing in this table is new. That is the point of learning the nouns first.

**The -ος/-α/-ο variant.** When the stem ends in a vowel or in **ρ**, the feminine is **-α** rather than **-η**:

- **ωραίος, ωραία, ωραίο** — lovely
- **νέος, νέα, νέο** — new, young
- **κρύος, κρύα, κρύο** — cold
- **μικρός, μικρή, μικρό** — small — but **καθαρός, καθαρή, καθαρό** keeps **-η**

**The rule is not perfectly tidy** and the deck stores each adjective's feminine. The tendency: a vowel before the ending gives **-α**, **ρ** gives either.

**Agreement is in all three at once** — gender, number and case:

- **ο καλός δάσκαλος** → **του καλού δασκάλου** → **τους καλούς δασκάλους**
- **η μεγάλη πόλη** → **της μεγάλης πόλης** → **τις μεγάλες πόλεις**
- **το μικρό παιδί** → **του μικρού παιδιού** → **τα μικρά παιδιά**

**Which means an adjective and its noun move together**, and getting one right and the other wrong is the commonest intermediate error. Practise them as pairs, never alone.

**Position: before the noun, inside the article.** **ο καλός δάσκαλος**. After the noun it becomes a predicate — **ο δάσκαλος είναι καλός** — or an emphatic construction: **ο δάσκαλος ο καλός**, *the teacher, the good one*, with both articles.

**Two or more adjectives** are joined with **και** or simply listed: **ένα μεγάλο, παλιό σπίτι** — a big old house.

**Practice.** Say the καλός table aloud twice, down the columns. Then put **μεγάλος** with **δρόμος, πόλη, σπίτι** in all four cases, singular and plural. Then say: *the good teacher's book · in the big city · of the small children · a big old house*.
More adjective patterns:
The patterns beyond **-ος/-η/-ο**, which cover a few hundred very common words — including the ones for *much*, *deep* and *sweet*.

**Pattern 1: -ύς / -ιά / -ύ.** Mostly adjectives of physical quality:

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | βαθύς | βαθιά | βαθύ |
| **Acc. sg.** | βαθύ | βαθιά | βαθύ |
| **Gen. sg.** | βαθιού | βαθιάς | βαθιού |
| **Nom. pl.** | βαθιοί | βαθιές | βαθιά |

**Words in it**: **βαθύς** (deep), **πλατύς** (wide), **μακρύς** (long), **βαρύς** (heavy), **ελαφρύς** (light), **γλυκός** — no, **γλυκός** is **-ος/-ιά/-ό**, a near neighbour: **γλυκός, γλυκιά, γλυκό** (sweet).

**Pattern 2: -ης / -ια / -ι.** A small set, mostly colours and characteristics:

- **σταχτής, σταχτιά, σταχτί** — grey
- **θαλασσής** — sea-blue
- **ζηλιάρης, ζηλιάρα, ζηλιάρικο** — jealous

**Pattern 3: -ων / -ουσα / -ον and -ής / -ής / -ές.** The learned patterns, from the older language, and they turn up in formal and scientific vocabulary: **ενδιαφέρων** (interesting), **διεθνής** (international), **ευγενής** (noble, polite), **συνεχής** (continuous). They are stage 9's register and worth recognising now: **ο διεθνής αερολιμένας** — the international airport, on a sign you will read.

**πολύς — much, many — is irregular and essential:**

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | πολύς | πολλή | πολύ |
| **Acc. sg.** | πολύ | πολλή | πολύ |
| **Nom. pl.** | πολλοί | πολλές | πολλά |
| **Acc. pl.** | πολλούς | πολλές | πολλά |

- **πολύς κόσμος** — a lot of people · **πολλή δουλειά** — a lot of work · **πολλά παιδιά** — many children
- **πολύ καλά** — very well. As an adverb, **πολύ** means *very* and does not change.

**Note the spelling: one λ in the singular masculine and neuter, two in everything else.** **πολύ** (very, much) against **πολλοί** (many) — a Spelling-track item.

**λίγος — a little, few — is regular**: **λίγος, λίγη, λίγο**, and **λίγο** as an adverb means *a little*: **Μιλάω λίγο ελληνικά.**

**όλος — all — takes the article after it**: **όλος ο κόσμος** (everyone, the whole world), **όλη η μέρα** (all day), **όλα τα παιδιά** (all the children). The article placement is the thing to notice.

**Practice.** Say the πολύς table aloud twice. Then say: **πολύς κόσμος · πολλή δουλειά · πολλά παιδιά · πολύ καλά · λίγο νερό · όλη η μέρα · όλα τα παιδιά**. Then put **βαθύς** with **θάλασσα** and **νερό** and check the feminine.
Comparatives:
*Bigger, better, more expensive* — and Greek gives you two ways to build them, one of which is almost always enough.

**Way one, and the one to use: πιο plus the adjective.**

- **πιο μεγάλος** — bigger · **πιο ακριβός** — more expensive · **πιο ωραία** — lovelier

**πιο never changes.** The adjective agrees with its noun as usual:

- **ένα πιο μεγάλο σπίτι** — a bigger house
- **μια πιο ωραία μέρα** — a lovelier day

**Way two: the -τερος ending.**

- **μεγάλος** → **μεγαλύτερος** · **ακριβός** → **ακριβότερος** · **μικρός** → **μικρότερος**

**Both are correct and they mean the same thing.** **πιο μεγάλος** and **μεγαλύτερος** are interchangeable; the **-τερος** forms are slightly more formal and are the ones that got fixed in common words. Use **πιο** by default and learn the **-τερος** forms you hear often.

**Than is από**, with the accusative:

- **Είναι πιο μεγάλος από μένα.** — He is bigger than me.
- **Η Αθήνα είναι πιο μεγάλη από τη Θεσσαλονίκη.** — Athens is bigger than Thessaloniki.
- **Είναι ακριβότερο από το άλλο.** — It is more expensive than the other.

**Or παρά, before a clause**: **Είναι καλύτερα να πας παρά να μείνεις** — it is better to go than to stay. **Από** for nouns and pronouns, **παρά** for alternatives.

**As...as: τόσο...όσο.**

- **Είναι τόσο μεγάλος όσο εγώ.** — He is as big as me.
- **όχι τόσο ακριβό** — not so expensive

**More and less, with nouns**: **πιο πολύ** or **περισσότερο** (more), **λιγότερο** (less):

- **Θέλω περισσότερο καφέ.** — I want more coffee.
- **Μιλάω λιγότερο από σένα.** — I speak less than you.

**The comparative adverb** is the neuter: **πιο καλά** or **καλύτερα** (better), **πιο γρήγορα** or **γρηγορότερα** (faster).

- **Μπορείς να μιλάς πιο αργά;** — Can you speak more slowly? — which you already know as a phrase and can now see the grammar of.

**The irregular ones are the next lesson**, and they are the four or five you will use most.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **πιο μεγάλος · πιο ακριβό · μεγαλύτερος · Είναι πιο μεγάλος από μένα · όχι τόσο ακριβό · πιο αργά**. Then compare five pairs of things out loud — your town and Athens, Greek and English, coffee and tea.
Superlatives:
*The biggest, the best* — and a second meaning of the same forms that English does with *very*.

**The relative superlative: the article plus the comparative.**

- **ο πιο μεγάλος** — the biggest · **το πιο ωραίο** — the loveliest
- **ο μεγαλύτερος** — the biggest, with the **-τερος** form

**With the group it is biggest of**, using **από** or a genitive:

- **Είναι ο πιο μεγάλος από όλους.** — He is the biggest of all.
- **η πιο μεγάλη πόλη της Ελλάδας** — the biggest city in Greece

**Note that English *in* becomes a genitive**: *the biggest city in Greece* is *the biggest city **of** Greece*. That is standard and the English version would be wrong.

**The absolute superlative: -τατος, meaning *very* rather than *most*.**

- **ωραιότατος** — extremely lovely · **μεγαλότατος**? no — **μέγιστος** (greatest), **ελάχιστος** (least)
- **πολύ ωραίος** is the ordinary way to say *very lovely*; **ωραιότατος** is emphatic and slightly literary.

**The learned superlatives you will meet** — and they are all over church and formal language, which is why they are here:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **μέγιστος** | greatest |
| **ελάχιστος** | least, minimal |
| **άριστος** | best, excellent |
| **ύψιστος** | highest — **Ύψιστε** in prayers |
| **Παναγιώτατος** | All-Holy — the Patriarch's style |
| **Σεβασμιώτατος** | Most Reverend — a bishop's |

**Those last two are superlatives doing social work**, and now you can see what they are made of: **πανάγιος** (all-holy) and **σεβάσμιος** (reverend) with the **-ότατος** superlative ending. The forms of address from the earlier lesson are grammar after all.

**The adverbial superlative**: **το πιο καλά**, or more usually **όσο πιο καλά μπορώ** — as well as I can.

**πάρα πολύ** is the everyday intensifier: **πάρα πολύ καλά** — very well indeed, **πάρα πολύ ακριβό** — far too expensive.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **ο πιο μεγάλος · η πιο μεγάλη πόλη της Ελλάδας · ο καλύτερος · πάρα πολύ ακριβό**. Then say: *the biggest city in Greece · the best coffee in the town · the oldest church here*. Then say **Σεβασμιώτατε** and **Παναγιώτατε** and name the adjective inside each.
The irregular comparatives:
Five adjectives whose comparatives are not built by rule — and they are five of the most used words in the language.

| Adjective | Comparative | Superlative |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **καλός** good | **καλύτερος** better | **ο καλύτερος** / **άριστος** |
| **κακός** bad | **χειρότερος** worse | **ο χειρότερος** |
| **πολύς** much | **περισσότερος** more | **ο περισσότερος** / **πλείστος** |
| **λίγος** little | **λιγότερος** less | **ο λιγότερος** / **ελάχιστος** |
| **μεγάλος** big | **μεγαλύτερος** bigger | **ο μεγαλύτερος** / **μέγιστος** |
| **μικρός** small | **μικρότερος** smaller | **ο μικρότερος** |

**The adverbs go with them:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **καλά** → **καλύτερα** | well → better |
| **κακά / άσχημα** → **χειρότερα** | badly → worse |
| **πολύ** → **περισσότερο** / **πιο πολύ** | much → more |
| **λίγο** → **λιγότερο** | a little → less |

**καλύτερα is one of the most useful words in Greek**, because it carries *better* in all its senses:

- **Είμαι καλύτερα.** — I am better. (health)
- **Καλύτερα να πάμε.** — We had better go.
- **Είναι καλύτερα έτσι.** — It is better this way.
- **Όσο καλύτερα μπορώ.** — As well as I can.

**χειρότερα likewise**: **πάει χειρότερα** — it is going worse.

**μεγαλύτερος of people means older**, not larger: **ο μεγαλύτερος αδελφός μου** — my older brother. And **μικρότερος** means younger. That is the normal way to say it; **πιο μεγάλος** would be heard the same way.

**Can you say πιο καλός?** Yes, and people do — **πιο καλός** and **πιο μεγάλος** are heard constantly alongside **καλύτερος** and **μεγαλύτερος**. Neither is wrong. The irregular forms are the more standard ones in writing.

**περισσότερος inflects like an adjective**: **περισσότερα παιδιά** (more children), **περισσότερη δουλειά** (more work), **οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι** (most people).

**οι περισσότεροι** on its own means *most people*, and **τα περισσότερα** *most things* — both extremely common.

**Practice.** Say the six rows aloud twice. Then say: **Είμαι καλύτερα · Καλύτερα να πάμε · ο μεγαλύτερος αδελφός μου · οι περισσότεροι άνθρωποι · πάει χειρότερα**. Then compare three things using an irregular comparative each time.
The pronouns in full:
All the pronouns, all the cases, in one place — the strong set, the weak set, and which is used where.

**The strong pronouns**, used for emphasis and after prepositions:

| | Nominative | Accusative | Genitive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | εγώ | εμένα | εμένα |
| you | εσύ | εσένα | εσένα |
| he | αυτός | αυτόν | αυτού |
| she | αυτή | αυτήν | αυτής |
| it | αυτό | αυτό | αυτού |
| we | εμείς | εμάς | εμάς |
| you (pl.) | εσείς | εσάς | εσάς |
| they (m) | αυτοί | αυτούς | αυτών |
| they (f) | αυτές | αυτές | αυτών |
| they (n) | αυτά | αυτά | αυτών |

**The weak pronouns**, which do the ordinary work:

| | Accusative (direct) | Genitive (indirect / possessive) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| me | με | μου |
| you | σε | σου |
| him | τον | του |
| her | την | της |
| it | το | του |
| us | μας | μας |
| you (pl.) | σας | σας |
| them (m) | τους | τους |
| them (f) | τις | τους |
| them (n) | τα | τους |

**Where each goes:**

1. **Weak accusative** — the direct object, before the verb: **Τον βλέπω.**
2. **Weak genitive** — the indirect object before the verb (**Μου λέει**) and the possessive after a noun (**ο φίλος μου**).
3. **Strong** — for emphasis (**Εμένα ρώτησε**), after prepositions (**για μένα**), and standing alone (**Ποιος; — Εγώ.**).

**Prepositions always take the strong forms**: **για μένα, με σένα, από αυτόν, σ' εμάς**. This is the test to apply when you are unsure which set to use — after a preposition, strong.

**Both together, with the order fixed**: indirect, then direct — **Μου το δίνει**, **Σου τα έστειλα**, **Της το είπα**.

**The reflexive: ο εαυτός μου.**

- **Βλέπω τον εαυτό μου.** — I see myself.
- **Μίλησε στον εαυτό του.** — He talked to himself.

**ο εαυτός is a noun** — *the self* — with a possessive attached, so it declines like a noun and the possessive tells you whose: **τον εαυτό μου, τον εαυτό σου, τον εαυτό της**.

**μόνος μου means *by myself***: **Πήγα μόνος μου** — I went on my own. It agrees: **μόνη μου** if you are female.

**ο ένας τον άλλον** is *each other*: **Βοηθάμε ο ένας τον άλλον** — we help each other.

**Practice.** Say both tables aloud, down the columns. Then say: **Τον βλέπω · Μου λέει · ο φίλος μου · για μένα · Εμένα ρώτησε · Μου το δίνει · Βλέπω τον εαυτό μου · Πήγα μόνος μου**. Then say five sentences where the pronoun is strong and five where it is weak, and name why each time.
που — the relative pronoun:
How Greek joins two clauses — and it is one word, unchanging, for *who*, *which* and *that*.

**που does all of it:**

- **ο άντρας που είδα** — the man **whom** I saw
- **η γυναίκα που μιλάει** — the woman **who** is speaking
- **το βιβλίο που διαβάζω** — the book **that** I am reading
- **το σπίτι που μένω** — the house **where** I live

**It never changes** — no gender, no case, no number. After the nouns and adjectives of the last few lessons, that is a relief and it is genuinely how the modern language works.

**And it is never omitted.** English drops it — *the book I am reading* — and Greek cannot: **το βιβλίο που διαβάζω**, always.

**Note the accent: που has none.** With an accent, **πού** is *where?*, the question word. The two are distinguished only by that mark, as the Spelling track said.

**Where English needs a preposition, Greek adds a pronoun:**

- **ο άντρας που του έδωσα το βιβλίο** — the man **to whom** I gave the book (*that I gave him the book*)
- **το σπίτι που μένω σε αυτό** — or more naturally **το σπίτι στο οποίο μένω**, with the formal relative

**That second case is where που runs out**, and it is why the next lesson exists.

**αυτό που means *what*, in the sense of *the thing that*:**

- **Αυτό που θέλω είναι...** — What I want is...
- **Δεν ξέρω αυτό που λες.** — I do not know what you are saying.
- **ό,τι** is the other way of saying it: **ό,τι θέλεις** — whatever you want. Note the comma inside it, which distinguishes it from **ότι** (*that*).

**ότι against ό,τι** is a real spelling distinction:

- **Ξέρω ότι είναι καλά.** — I know **that** he is well.
- **Κάνε ό,τι θέλεις.** — Do **whatever** you want.

**όπου, όποτε, όπως** are the same idea for place, time and manner: **όπου θέλεις** (wherever you like), **όποτε μπορείς** (whenever you can), **όπως θέλεις** (however you like, as you like).

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **ο άντρας που είδα · το βιβλίο που διαβάζω · Αυτό που θέλω · Ξέρω ότι είναι καλά · Κάνε ό,τι θέλεις**. Then join five pairs of short sentences with **που**, out loud. Then write **ότι** and **ό,τι** in two sentences and say which is which.
ο οποίος, and when it is needed:
The formal relative pronoun, which inflects — and the two situations where **που** cannot do the job.

**The forms**, which are the adjective endings again:

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom. sg.** | ο οποίος | η οποία | το οποίο |
| **Acc. sg.** | τον οποίο | την οποία | το οποίο |
| **Gen. sg.** | του οποίου | της οποίας | του οποίου |
| **Nom. pl.** | οι οποίοι | οι οποίες | τα οποία |

**When it is necessary**, and there are two cases:

**1. After a preposition.**

- **το σπίτι στο οποίο μένω** — the house in which I live
- **ο άνθρωπος με τον οποίο μίλησα** — the person with whom I spoke
- **η εταιρεία για την οποία δουλεύω** — the company I work for

**που cannot take a preposition**, so formal and written Greek uses **ο οποίος** here. Spoken Greek restructures instead: **το σπίτι που μένω**, **ο άνθρωπος που μίλησα μαζί του**.

**2. Where που would be ambiguous.**

- **ο γιος του δασκάλου, ο οποίος είναι δάσκαλος και αυτός** — the teacher's son, who is also a teacher. With **που**, it is unclear which of the two is meant; **ο οποίος** is masculine singular nominative and so can only be the son.

**That disambiguation is its real use**, and it is why formal writing — law, journalism, academic Greek — uses it heavily while speech barely does.

**του οποίου is the formal whose:**

- **ο άντρας του οποίου το σπίτι κάηκε** — the man whose house burned down
- Spoken: **ο άντρας που κάηκε το σπίτι του**

**The register point.** **Ο οποίος** is correct, useful and slightly formal. Using it constantly in speech sounds like a newsreader; never using it in writing sounds unlettered. The practical rule for you: understand it everywhere, use it after prepositions in writing, and use **που** when you talk.

**οποίος without the article** means *whoever*: **όποιος θέλει** — whoever wants. Note the accent shift: **όποιος** with the accent on the first syllable is *whoever*; **ο οποίος** with the article is *who, which*.

**Practice.** Say the table aloud. Then convert three sentences from **που** to **ο οποίος** and back: *the house I live in · the man I spoke to · the book I am reading*. Then read a Greek news sentence and find its **ο οποίος**.
όλος, κάποιος, κανένας, τίποτα:
The indefinite words — *all, some, any, none, nothing, other, same* — and the two of them that need **δεν** to work.

**όλος — all, whole.** It takes the article **after** it:

- **όλος ο κόσμος** — everyone, the whole world
- **όλη η μέρα** — all day
- **όλα τα παιδιά** — all the children
- **όλοι** on its own — everybody · **όλα** — everything

**κάποιος — someone, some.** Inflects like an adjective:

- **κάποιος ρώτησε** — someone asked
- **κάποια μέρα** — some day
- **κάτι** — something, and it does not inflect: **κάτι άλλο** (something else)

**κανένας / καμία / κανένα — nobody, none, any.** This one does two opposite jobs:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν ήρθε κανένας.** | Nobody came. — with δεν |
| **Ήρθε κανένας;** | Did anybody come? — in a question |
| **Δεν έχω καμία ιδέα.** | I have no idea. |
| **Θέλεις κανένα καφέ;** | Would you like a coffee? — *any* coffee, idiomatically |

**τίποτα — nothing, anything.** The same pattern:

- **Δεν θέλω τίποτα.** — I do not want anything.
- **Θέλεις τίποτα;** — Do you want anything?
- **Τίποτα!** — Nothing! — and also *you're welcome*, informally.

**Both need δεν for the negative meaning**, as stage 2's negation lesson said. **Δεν ξέρω τίποτα** is *I know nothing*; **ξέρω τίποτα** is not a sentence.

**πουθενά — nowhere, anywhere**: **Δεν πάω πουθενά.**

**ποτέ — never, ever**: **Δεν πάω ποτέ.** · **Πήγες ποτέ;** — Have you ever been?

**άλλος — other, another.** Inflects, and takes the article as needed:

- **ο άλλος** — the other one · **ένας άλλος** — another one · **άλλα παιδιά** — other children
- **κάτι άλλο;** — anything else? — the shop question from stage 2

**ίδιος — same, self.**

- **ο ίδιος άνθρωπος** — the same person
- **ο ίδιος ο παπάς** — the priest himself
- **το ίδιο** — the same thing. **Το ίδιο κάνει.** — It makes no difference.

**μερικοί — some, a few** (plural only): **μερικά παιδιά** — some children.

**καθένας — each one**: **καθένας ξέρει** — everyone knows. And **κάθε** — every, invariable: **κάθε μέρα** (every day), **κάθε Κυριακή** (every Sunday).

**κάθε Κυριακή is worth having now**, because it is how you will describe your own week.

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **όλη η μέρα · όλα τα παιδιά · κάποιος ρώτησε · Δεν ήρθε κανένας · Δεν θέλω τίποτα · κάτι άλλο; · ο ίδιος ο παπάς · κάθε Κυριακή**. Then say five sentences about your week using **κάθε**, **όλος** and **μερικοί**.
Numbers in the other cases, and the ordi:
Numbers inflect less than anything else in Greek — but the ones that do inflect are the ones you use most, and the ordinals behave like adjectives.

**The cardinals that inflect: 1, 3, 4** and the hundreds and thousands.

| | Masculine | Feminine | Neuter |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **1 nom.** | ένας | μία | ένα |
| **1 acc.** | έναν | μία | ένα |
| **1 gen.** | ενός | μιας | ενός |
| **3** | τρεις | τρεις | τρία |
| **3 gen.** | τριών | τριών | τριών |
| **4** | τέσσερις | τέσσερις | τέσσερα |
| **4 gen.** | τεσσάρων | τεσσάρων | τεσσάρων |

**τριών and τεσσάρων** are the forms to notice, because they appear in dates, ages and measures: **τριών χρονών** (three years old), **τεσσάρων ημερών** (of four days).

**δύο never changes**, nor does anything from 5 to 100 except the hundreds: **πέντε, δέκα, είκοσι** are fixed.

**The hundreds inflect for gender**: **διακόσιοι άντρες, διακόσιες γυναίκες, διακόσια παιδιά**. **Χίλιοι, χίλιες, χίλια** likewise.

**The ordinals are ordinary adjectives** in **-ος / -η / -ο**:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **πρώτος** | first | **έκτος** | sixth |
| **δεύτερος** | second | **έβδομος** | seventh |
| **τρίτος** | third | **όγδοος** | eighth |
| **τέταρτος** | fourth | **ένατος** | ninth |
| **πέμπτος** | fifth | **δέκατος** | tenth |

**And they inflect fully**: **ο πρώτος όροφος** (the first floor), **στην πρώτη σελίδα** (on the first page), **του δεύτερου παιδιού** (of the second child).

**Where you need them:**

- **The days of the week**, which are ordinals: **Δευτέρα, Τρίτη, Τετάρτη, Πέμπτη** — second, third, fourth, fifth.
- **Floors**: **ο πρώτος όροφος**, **το ισόγειο** (ground floor).
- **The first of the month**: **την πρώτη Μαΐου**.
- **Church ordinals**, constantly: **η Δευτέρα Παρουσία** (the Second Coming), **η Πρώτη Οικουμενική Σύνοδος** (the First Ecumenical Council), **ο Τρίτος Ανάστασιμος Ήχος**? — the tones are numbered **Α΄ to Πλ. Δ΄**, which is the alphabetic numeral from stage 1.

**Fractions**: **μισό** (half), **ένα τρίτο** (a third), **ένα τέταρτο** (a quarter) — and **μισή ώρα** (half an hour), **ένα τέταρτο** again for a quarter of an hour.

**Once, twice, three times**: **μία φορά, δύο φορές, τρεις φορές** — and **πολλές φορές** (many times), **καμιά φορά** (sometimes), **άλλη φορά** (another time).

**Practice.** Say the genitives **ενός, μιας, τριών, τεσσάρων** aloud. Then say the ten ordinals. Then say: *the first floor · on the first of May · three years old · twice · sometimes · the second child's name*.
The neuter nouns in -ος, and other survi:
The nouns that look like they belong to another gender, and the handful of irregulars worth learning as whole patterns. All of them are survivors of the ancient third declension.

**The neuter -ος nouns:**

| | Singular | Plural |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nom./acc.** | το δάσος | τα δάση |
| **Genitive** | του δάσους | των δασών |

**The set**, and it is small and common: **το δάσος** (forest), **το μέρος** (part, place), **το έθνος** (nation), **το κράτος** (state), **το έτος** (year, formal), **το πλήθος** (crowd), **το βάρος** (weight), **το μέγεθος** (size), **το πάθος** (passion), **το ήθος** (character), **το τέλος** (end).

**How to tell them from masculine -ος nouns:** by the article, and nothing else. **ο δρόμος** against **το δάσος**. So these are exactly the nouns where learning the article with the word is not optional.

**The English evidence is everywhere**: *ethnos* in *ethnic*, *kratos* in *democracy*, *pathos*, *ethos*, *telos* in *teleology*. All of them came into English in this neuter form.

**The -ας and -ως neuters**, a smaller set: **το κρέας** (meat) → **του κρέατος, τα κρέατα**; **το φως** (light) → **του φωτός, τα φώτα**; **το γάλα** (milk) → **του γάλακτος**; **το γεγονός** (event) → **του γεγονότος**.

**το φως and το γάλα are worth knowing cold**, because you will say both constantly, and their genitives explain English words: **φωτός** → *photo-*, **γάλακτος** → *galaxy*, *lactose*.

**The nouns that are simply irregular:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο άνθρωπος** → **οι άνθρωποι** | regular, but note the stress shift to **ανθρώπων** |
| **η γυναίκα** → **των γυναικών** | the genitive plural loses the **ε** |
| **ο γιος** → **του γιου, οι γιοι** | short and irregular |
| **η μητέρα** / **ο πατέρας** | regular, and the vocatives **μητέρα! πατέρα!** are what you use |
| **το παιδί** → **του παιδιού** | regular **-ι**, with the stress on the ending |
| **ο καφές** → **του καφέ, οι καφέδες** | its own small pattern, with **-έδες** |
| **η οδός** → **της οδού, οι οδοί** | feminine with masculine endings |
| **ο μήνας** → **του μήνα**, formal **του μηνός** | two genitives, and **του μηνός** is in the date phrase |

**Why they are irregular: because they are old.** Every one of these is a high-frequency word that kept an ancient form while the rest of the language regularised. That is the same reason English has *children* and *feet*, and it means the irregulars are always the common words — which is inconvenient and also means you meet them early and often.

**The deck stores each of these as a full pattern** rather than as a rule, because there is no rule.

**Practice.** Give all four forms of **το δάσος**, **το φως** and **ο καφές**. Then say: **στο δάσος · το φως του ηλίου · δύο καφέδες · της οδού Ερμού**. Then take five nouns from the deck and say which declension pattern each belongs to.
Word order, now that the cases do the wo:
Stage 2 said Greek word order can move. Now that you have the cases, this lesson is what moving it actually does.

**The neutral order is subject, verb, object** — but only about half of Greek sentences are in it, and the rest are not disordered.

**What moving the subject does: it makes the verb the news.**

- **Ο Γιώργος ήρθε.** — George came. (neutral)
- **Ήρθε ο Γιώργος.** — George **came** / **George** came — the arrival is the point, or George is new information.

**Verb-first is extremely common**, and especially when introducing something:

- **Ήρθε ένας άντρας.** — A man came.
- **Υπάρχει ένα πρόβλημα.** — There is a problem.
- **Μου αρέσει ο καφές.** — I like coffee. (the thing liked follows the verb)

**What moving the object to the front does: it contrasts it.**

- **Τον καφέ τον θέλω σκέτο.** — The coffee, I want it without sugar. (as against other things)
- **Τα παιδιά τα πήγα στο σχολείο.** — The children, I took them to school.

**Note the doubled pronoun** in those: when a noun is moved to the front, Greek usually repeats it as a weak pronoun before the verb. **Τον καφέ τον θέλω** — *the coffee, I want it*. That doubling is a marker of topicalisation and it is entirely normal.

**The given-new principle**, which is the underlying rule: what the listener already knows comes first, and the new information comes later. English does this with stress and with constructions like *it was George who came*; Greek does it with order.

**The adjective's position matters too:**

- **ο καλός δάσκαλος** — the good teacher (neutral)
- **ο δάσκαλος ο καλός** — the teacher, the good one (emphatic, contrastive)
- **ο δάσκαλος είναι καλός** — the teacher is good (predicate)

**What cannot move:**

1. **The weak pronouns.** Immediately before the verb, in a fixed order, always — **μου το δίνει**, never *το μου δίνει*.
2. **δεν**, which stays directly before the pronoun-plus-verb cluster.
3. **The article**, which stays with its noun.
4. **Prepositions**, which stay before their noun.

**So the moveable parts are the whole phrases** — subject, object, adverbials — and the glued parts are the little words around the verb.

**Why this matters for listening more than for speaking.** You can speak neutral Greek all your life and be understood perfectly. But you have to **hear** the other orders, because a verb-first sentence or a fronted object will otherwise sound like a mistake, and a doubled pronoun will sound like a stutter.

**Practice.** Say these three ways each and name the emphasis: **Ο Γιώργος ήρθε / Ήρθε ο Γιώργος** · **Θέλω τον καφέ σκέτο / Τον καφέ τον θέλω σκέτο**. Then listen to one Easy Greek clip and count how many sentences begin with the verb.
Quantities, containers and measures:
How to ask for amounts of things, which is most of what you do in a shop or at a table.

**The measures:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ένα κιλό** | a kilo | **μισό κιλό** | half a kilo |
| **ένα τέταρτο** | a quarter (kilo) | **εκατό γραμμάρια** | 100 grams |
| **ένα λίτρο** | a litre | **μισό λίτρο** | half a litre |
| **ένα μέτρο** | a metre | **ένα χιλιόμετρο** | a kilometre |

**The containers, which are how drinks and portions are counted:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ένα ποτήρι** | a glass | **ένα φλιτζάνι** | a cup |
| **ένα μπουκάλι** | a bottle | **μια κούπα** | a mug |
| **ένα πιάτο** | a plate | **ένα κουτί** | a box, a tin |
| **μια σακούλα** | a bag | **μια μερίδα** | a portion |
| **ένα κομμάτι** | a piece | **μια φέτα** | a slice |

**No preposition between the measure and the thing**, which is the grammatical point:

- **ένα κιλό ψωμί** — a kilo of bread. Not *ένα κιλό από ψωμί*.
- **ένα ποτήρι νερό** — a glass of water
- **μια μερίδα σουβλάκι** — a portion of souvlaki
- **δύο φέτες τυρί** — two slices of cheese

**The thing stays in the accusative**, as the object of the sentence, and the measure simply precedes it. This differs from English, which needs *of*, and from the genitive you might expect — Greek does not use one here.

**The quantity words:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **λίγο** | a little — **λίγο ψωμί** |
| **πολύ** | a lot — **πολύ νερό** |
| **αρκετά** | enough, quite a lot |
| **τόσο** | this much — **τόσο, παρακαλώ**, with a gesture |
| **περισσότερο / λιγότερο** | more / less |
| **ακόμα λίγο** | a bit more |
| **φτάνει** | that's enough (*it reaches*) |
| **μόνο** | only |

**φτάνει is the word to have ready** when someone is filling your plate, and in a Greek house you will need it: **Φτάνει, ευχαριστώ!** — and expect to be ignored once.

**At the table:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλή όρεξη!** | enjoy your meal |
| **Στην υγειά μας!** | to our health — the toast |
| **Είναι πολύ νόστιμο.** | it is very tasty |
| **Δεν μπορώ άλλο.** | I cannot manage any more |
| **Είμαι χορτάτος / χορτάτη.** | I am full |

**Practice.** Say these aloud: **ένα κιλό ψωμί · ένα ποτήρι νερό · δύο φέτες τυρί · λίγο λάδι · φτάνει, ευχαριστώ · Καλή όρεξη**. Then order a full meal out loud, with quantities. Then refuse a second helping politely, twice.
Weather, and the impersonal verbs:
Verbs with no subject — the weather, and a small set of extremely common expressions that work the same way.

**The weather uses κάνει — *it makes*:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κάνει ζέστη.** | It is hot. |
| **Κάνει κρύο.** | It is cold. |
| **Κάνει καλό καιρό.** | The weather is good. |
| **Κάνει άσχημο καιρό.** | The weather is bad. |
| **Κάνει πολλή ζέστη.** | It is very hot. |

**And its own verbs for precipitation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Βρέχει.** | It is raining. |
| **Χιονίζει.** | It is snowing. |
| **Φυσάει.** | It is windy. |
| **Αστράφτει. Βροντάει.** | There is lightning. It is thundering. |

**Those have no subject at all** — no word for *it* — because Greek does not need one, as stage 2's pronoun lesson said.

**The weather nouns, for forecasts and conversation:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο καιρός** | the weather | **ο ήλιος** | the sun |
| **η βροχή** | rain | **το χιόνι** | snow |
| **ο αέρας** | wind, air | **η ζέστη** | heat |
| **το κρύο** | cold | **η υγρασία** | humidity |
| **η θερμοκρασία** | temperature | **τα σύννεφα** | clouds |

- **Τι καιρό κάνει;** — What is the weather like?
- **Έχει ήλιο.** — It is sunny. (*it has sun*)
- **Έχει συννεφιά.** — It is cloudy.

**The other impersonal verbs**, which are not about weather and are used constantly:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **πρέπει** | it is necessary, must — **Πρέπει να πάω** (I must go) |
| **μπορεί** | it may, perhaps — **Μπορεί να βρέξει** (it may rain) |
| **αρκεί** | it is enough |
| **φαίνεται** | it seems |
| **συμβαίνει** | it happens — **Τι συμβαίνει;** (what is happening?) |
| **χρειάζεται** | it is needed |
| **απαγορεύεται** | it is forbidden — on every sign in Greece |

**πρέπει is the important one.** It never changes form: **πρέπει να πάω, πρέπει να πας, πρέπει να πάμε** — the person is carried by the second verb, not by **πρέπει**. That construction with **να** is stage 4's subject and this is a usable preview.

- **Πρέπει να φύγω.** — I must go.
- **Δεν πρέπει να το κάνεις.** — You must not do that.
- **Τι πρέπει να κάνω;** — What should I do?

**απαγορεύεται is worth recognising** because it is on signs everywhere: **Απαγορεύεται το κάπνισμα** (no smoking), **Απαγορεύεται η είσοδος** (no entry).

**Practice.** Say the weather for today, out loud, three ways. Then say: **Τι καιρό κάνει; · Κάνει πολλή ζέστη · Βρέχει · Μπορεί να βρέξει · Πρέπει να πάω**. Then say five things you must do today with **πρέπει να**.
Describing a person:
A production lesson: enough vocabulary and enough grammar to say what someone is like, which is one of the first things anyone will ask you to do.

**Physically:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ψηλός** | tall | **κοντός** | short |
| **αδύνατος** | thin | **χοντρός** | fat |
| **νέος** | young | **μεγάλος** | older |
