| **το μάθημα** | lesson, subject | **η τάξη** | class, classroom, year |
| **το θρανίο** | desk | **ο πίνακας** | board |
| **το τετράδιο** | exercise book | **το βιβλίο** | book |
| **οι εξετάσεις** | exams | **ο βαθμός** | mark, grade |
| **η εργασία** | homework, assignment | **το διάλειμμα** | break |
| **το πτυχίο** | degree | **οι πανελλήνιες** | the national university entrance exams |

**The subjects**, since the readers are one of them:

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **τα ελληνικά / η γλώσσα** | Greek | **τα μαθηματικά** | maths |
| **η ιστορία** | history | **η γεωγραφία** | geography |
| **η φυσική** | physics | **η χημεία** | chemistry |
| **τα θρησκευτικά** | religious education | **η γυμναστική** | PE |
| **η μουσική** | music | **τα αγγλικά** | English |

**τα θρησκευτικά is taught in Greek state schools** as Orthodox Christianity, which is a fact worth knowing for conversation.

**Talking about your own learning**, which is what you will do most:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μαθαίνω ελληνικά.** | I am learning Greek. |
| **Μαθαίνω μόνος μου.** | I am teaching myself. |
| **Διαβάζω κάθε μέρα.** | I study every day. |
| **Έχω ένα πρόγραμμα.** | I have a programme. |
| **Μαθαίνω έναν χρόνο.** | I have been learning for a year. |
| **Το δύσκολο είναι τα ρήματα.** | The hard part is the verbs. |
| **Καταλαβαίνω πιο καλά απ' ό,τι μιλάω.** | I understand better than I speak. |

**That last sentence is true of every learner** and saying it saves a lot of explanation.

**Practice.** Say the seven sentences about your own learning aloud. Then name the six years of **δημοτικό** with their alphabetic numerals. Then say which school subject you were best at, in the imperfect: **Μου άρεσε η ιστορία.**
The family, in full:
The relations, including the in-laws and the godparents — because Greek family vocabulary is more precise than English and the relationships matter more socially.

**The close family:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο πατέρας / ο μπαμπάς** | father / dad | **η μητέρα / η μαμά** | mother / mum |
| **ο γιος** | son | **η κόρη** | daughter |
| **ο αδελφός** | brother | **η αδελφή** | sister |
| **ο παππούς** | grandfather | **η γιαγιά** | grandmother |
| **ο εγγονός** | grandson | **η εγγονή** | granddaughter |
| **ο σύζυγος / ο άντρας** | husband | **η σύζυγος / η γυναίκα** | wife |
| **τα παιδιά** | children | **τα εγγόνια** | grandchildren |
| **οι γονείς** | parents | **τα αδέλφια** | siblings |

**The wider family:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ο θείος** | uncle | **η θεία** | aunt |
| **ο ανιψιός** | nephew | **η ανιψιά** | niece |
| **ο ξάδελφος** | cousin (m) | **η ξαδέλφη** | cousin (f) |
| **ο συγγενής** | relative | **η οικογένεια** | family |
| **το σόι** | the extended family, the clan | | |

**The in-laws**, which English handles with *-in-law* and Greek with separate words:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο πεθερός / η πεθερά** | father-in-law / mother-in-law |
| **ο γαμπρός** | son-in-law — and *bridegroom* |
| **η νύφη** | daughter-in-law — and *bride* |
| **ο κουνιάδος / η κουνιάδα** | brother- / sister-in-law |
| **τα συμπέθερα** | the two sets of parents, to each other |

**τα συμπέθερα has no English word at all** — the relationship between your parents and your spouse's parents — and it is a real and named relationship in Greek life.

**The spiritual family**, which is the part that matters most in a parish:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **ο νονός / η νονά** | godfather / godmother |
| **το βαφτιστήρι** | godchild |
| **ο κουμπάρος / η κουμπάρα** | wedding sponsor — and the godparent of your child |
| **η κουμπαριά** | the relationship itself |

**κουμπαριά is a kinship, not a courtesy.** The man who sponsors your wedding or baptises your child is **ο κουμπάρος μου** for life, the relationship is treated as family, and the word is used as a greeting between men who stand in it. In some places it creates an impediment to marriage between the families, which tells you how seriously it is taken.

**Talking about them:**

- **Έχω δύο αδέλφια, έναν αδελφό και μια αδελφή.**
- **Ο πατέρας μου είναι από…**
- **Η γυναίκα μου είναι Ελληνίδα / Αγγλίδα.**
- **Τα παιδιά μου πάνε σχολείο εδώ.**
- **Ο νονός του παιδιού μου είναι ο Γιώργος.**
- **Όλο το σόι θα είναι εκεί.**

**The question you will be asked** is **Έχεις οικογένεια;** — which means *are you married with children*, and not *do you have relatives*.

**Practice.** Draw your own family and name every member in Greek, out loud, with the right article and relation. Then say who is whose — using genitives — for five of them. Then learn **κουμπάρος** and **νονός** properly, because you will hear both this month.
Feelings and opinions:
How you feel and what you think — which is what moves a conversation past facts, and which Greek does with a small set of constructions you already have.

**Feelings — mostly with είμαι or the mediopassive:**

| | | | |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **χαρούμενος** | happy | **λυπημένος** | sad |
| **κουρασμένος** | tired | **θυμωμένος** | angry |
| **ανήσυχος** | worried | **ήρεμος** | calm |
| **ενθουσιασμένος** | excited | **απογοητευμένος** | disappointed |
| **νευρικός** | on edge | **ευτυχισμένος** | happy, blessed |
| **μπερδεμένος** | confused | **περήφανος** | proud |

- **Είμαι κουρασμένος.** — I am tired. (and **κουρασμένη** if you are female)
- **Χαίρομαι πολύ.** — I am very glad.
- **Λυπάμαι.** — I am sorry.
- **Ανησυχώ.** — I am worried.
- **Φοβάμαι.** — I am afraid.
- **Νιώθω καλά / άσχημα.** — I feel good / bad.

**νιώθω — I feel — is the verb for all of it** and takes an adverb: **νιώθω καλά, νιώθω κουρασμένος**.

**Opinions, and the four openers:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Νομίζω ότι…** | I think that… |
| **Πιστεύω ότι…** | I believe that… |
| **Μου φαίνεται ότι…** | It seems to me that… |
| **Κατά τη γνώμη μου…** | In my opinion… |

**Νομίζω ότι is the everyday one** and it is followed by an ordinary clause with no change of mood — **Νομίζω ότι είναι καλό**.

**Strength of opinion:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Σίγουρα.** | Certainly. |
| **Μάλλον.** | Probably, rather. |
| **Ίσως.** | Perhaps. |
| **Μπορεί.** | Maybe. |
| **Δεν είμαι σίγουρος.** | I am not sure. |
| **Δεν ξέρω.** | I do not know. |
| **Δεν νομίζω.** | I do not think so. |
| **Έτσι νομίζω.** | I think so. |
| **Οπωσδήποτε!** | Absolutely! |

**Reacting, which is half of a conversation:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Αλήθεια;** | Really? |
| **Σοβαρά;** | Seriously? |
| **Τι ωραία!** | How lovely! |
| **Κρίμα.** | What a shame. |
| **Μπράβο!** | Well done! |
| **Πω πω!** | Wow! / Oh dear! — tone decides |
| **Δόξα τω Θεώ.** | Thank God. |
| **Ευτυχώς.** | Fortunately. |
| **Δυστυχώς.** | Unfortunately. |
| **Τι να κάνουμε;** | What can you do? — the Greek shrug |

**Τι να κάνουμε; and Δόξα τω Θεώ are the two most Greek responses on that list**, and between them they cover most of life: resignation and gratitude.

**Practice.** Say how you feel today in three ways. Then give your opinion on five things with four different openers. Then say all ten reactions aloud, with the right tone for each.
Agreeing and disagreeing:
How to take a side without being rude, which in Greek is less delicate than in English — argument is normal and warm.

**Agreeing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συμφωνώ.** | I agree. |
| **Ακριβώς!** | Exactly! |
| **Έτσι είναι.** | That's how it is. |
| **Σωστά.** | Right. |
| **Έχεις δίκιο.** | You are right. |
| **Και εγώ το ίδιο.** | Me too. |
| **Βεβαίως.** | Of course. |
| **Πολύ σωστά.** | Quite right. |
| **Δεν έχω αντίρρηση.** | I have no objection. |

**Έχεις δίκιο — *you have right* — is the standard** and it is said generously, including when the speaker is about to disagree anyway.

**Disagreeing:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν συμφωνώ.** | I do not agree. |
| **Διαφωνώ.** | I disagree. |
| **Δεν νομίζω.** | I do not think so. |
| **Δεν είναι έτσι.** | It is not like that. |
| **Έχεις άδικο.** | You are wrong. |
| **Δεν είμαι σίγουρος.** | I am not sure. |
| **Ναι, αλλά…** | Yes, but… |
| **Από μια πλευρά, ναι.** | In one way, yes. |
| **Εξαρτάται.** | It depends. |

**Εξαρτάται and Από μια πλευρά are the diplomatic ones** and they are what you reach for when you do not want the argument.

**Softening a disagreement:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Με συγχωρείς, αλλά…** | Forgive me, but… |
| **Δεν ξέρω, ίσως…** | I do not know, perhaps… |
| **Μπορεί να έχεις δίκιο, αλλά…** | You may be right, but… |
| **Καταλαβαίνω τι λες, όμως…** | I understand what you are saying, however… |

**The cultural note, and it is worth having before your first parish-hall argument:** Greeks argue loudly, interrupt freely, and do not take disagreement as hostility. A conversation about politics, football or the Church at raised volume between two men who then have coffee together is completely normal. Reading it as a quarrel is the English mistake.

**And the two phrases that end an argument amicably:**

- **Τέλος πάντων.** — Anyway. / Be that as it may.
- **Ας το αφήσουμε.** — Let's leave it.

**Τέλος πάντων is the universal subject-changer** and it is extremely useful when you have run out of Greek mid-argument.

**The topics that will come up**, so that you are not ambushed: Greek politics, the Church, the economy, football, the neighbours, immigration, and whether things were better before. You are not required to have views. **Δεν ξέρω αρκετά** — I do not know enough — is an honest and perfectly acceptable answer, and **Είμαι ξένος, ακούω και μαθαίνω** — I am a foreigner, I listen and learn — is even better.

**Practice.** Say nine agreements and nine disagreements aloud. Then take a position on something trivial and defend it for a minute in Greek, out loud. Then end it with **Τέλος πάντων** and change the subject.
Small talk, Greek style:
The conversation that fills the gaps, which in Greece follows a recognisable script — and knowing the script means you can participate before you can really talk.

**The opening sequence**, which happens nearly every time:

— **Γεια σου, τι κάνεις;**
— **Καλά, εσύ;**
— **Καλά, δόξα τω Θεώ.**
— **Τι νέα;**
— **Τίποτα ιδιαίτερο.**

**Τι νέα; — what's new — is asked constantly**, and **Τίποτα ιδιαίτερο** (nothing special) or **Όλα καλά** (all good) is the standard answer. Neither party expects news.

**The topics, in the order they usually arrive:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The weather** | **Τι ζέστη! · Τι κρύο κάνει! · Καλό καιρό έχουμε.** |
| **Health** | **Πώς είσαι; · Η υγεία σου;** and the answer **Δόξα τω Θεώ** |
| **Family** | **Τι κάνουν τα παιδιά; · Η γυναίκα σου;** |
| **Work** | **Πώς πάει η δουλειά; · Έχεις πολλή δουλειά;** |
| **Food** | **Έφαγες; · Τι έφαγες;** — asked with genuine interest |
| **The news** | **Είδες τι έγινε;** |
| **Whether you are warm, fed and well** | repeatedly, by older women especially |

**Έφαγες; — have you eaten? — is a real question** and a form of care, and answering **Όχι ακόμα** will often produce food.

**The things people say that have no information in them** and are the social glue:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι να σου πω.** | What can I tell you. |
| **Έτσι είναι η ζωή.** | That's life. |
| **Τι να κάνουμε;** | What can you do? |
| **Ο Θεός βοηθός.** | God help us. |
| **Με το καλό.** | May it go well. |
| **Καλή δύναμη.** | Strength to you. |
| **Σιγά σιγά.** | Slowly, slowly. |
| **Πάει ο καιρός.** | How time passes. |
| **Όλα θα πάνε καλά.** | It will all be fine. |

**Those nine are worth memorising as a set**, because they are what you say when you have nothing to say, and having them means a silence does not end the conversation.

**The compliments, which are given freely:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Μπράβο σου!** | Well done you! |
| **Τι ωραία που μιλάς ελληνικά!** | How nicely you speak Greek! |
| **Πολύ καλά τα λες.** | You say it very well. |
| **Μαθαίνεις γρήγορα.** | You are learning fast. |

**You will get all four of these**, often for very little Greek, and the correct response is **Ευχαριστώ, προσπαθώ** — thank you, I am trying — or **Σιγά σιγά**. Dismissing a Greek compliment is the English instinct and it falls flat; accepting it gracefully is the right move.

**Leaving:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πάω, γιατί έχω δουλειά.** | I'll go, I have things to do. |
| **Να τα πούμε.** | Let's talk again. |
| **Τα λέμε!** | See you! |
| **Χαιρετισμούς στην οικογένεια.** | Regards to the family. |
| **Να 'σαι καλά.** | Be well. |
| **Καλή συνέχεια.** | Have a good rest of the day. |

**Χαιρετισμούς στην οικογένεια is the standard parting courtesy** and it is noticed when a foreigner uses it.

**Practice.** Do the opening sequence aloud, both parts, ten times, until it is automatic. Then say the nine fillers and the six partings. Then have a two-minute conversation with yourself that contains no information at all.
Invitations: accepting and refusing:
Being invited, which will happen more than you expect — and refusing without offence, which is the harder half.

**The invitations:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Έλα σπίτι το βράδυ.** | Come round this evening. |
| **Πάμε για καφέ;** | Shall we go for a coffee? |
| **Θα πάμε για φαγητό. Θέλεις να έρθεις;** | We're going out to eat. Want to come? |
| **Σε περιμένουμε την Κυριακή.** | We'll expect you on Sunday. |
| **Έχουμε τραπέζι την Κυριακή. Θα έρθεις;** | We're having people over on Sunday. Will you come? |
| **Πέρασε από το σπίτι.** | Drop round. |
| **Σε θέλουμε στο γλέντι.** | We want you at the celebration. |
| **Μη φέρεις τίποτα!** | Don't bring anything! |

**Έχουμε τραπέζι — *we have a table* — is a meal with people**, and an invitation to one is a significant courtesy.

**Μη φέρεις τίποτα is said and not meant.** Bring something: a sweet from the **ζαχαροπλαστείο**, a bottle, flowers, or fruit. Arriving empty-handed is the error, and the instruction not to is a politeness.

**Accepting:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Ευχαρίστως!** | With pleasure! |
| **Θα έρθω, βεβαίως.** | I will come, of course. |
| **Πολύ ευχαρίστως, τι ώρα;** | Gladly — what time? |
| **Να φέρω κάτι;** | Shall I bring something? |
| **Ανυπομονώ.** | I am looking forward to it. |

**Ευχαρίστως is the one-word yes** to any invitation and it is warmer than **ναι**.

**Refusing, which needs a reason:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Δεν μπορώ, δυστυχώς.** | I cannot, unfortunately. |
| **Έχω κάτι άλλο εκείνη την ώρα.** | I have something else at that time. |
| **Θα ήθελα, αλλά δεν μπορώ.** | I would like to, but I cannot. |
| **Την άλλη φορά σίγουρα.** | Next time for certain. |
| **Συγγνώμη, είμαι κουρασμένος.** | Sorry, I am tired. |
| **Να το κανονίσουμε άλλη μέρα;** | Shall we arrange another day? |

**A bare no is not enough.** Greek refusals carry a reason and a counter-offer, and **Την άλλη φορά σίγουρα** does most of the work. Refusing twice in a row to the same person needs a third response that is an invitation of your own.

**And the Greek insistence**, which you should expect: an invitation refused once will be repeated, warmly, two or three times. That is not pressure, it is the form, and **Αλήθεια δεν μπορώ, αλλά ευχαριστώ πολύ** is the way out.

**The invitation you should make**, because reciprocity is how this works:

- **Ελάτε εσείς την άλλη Κυριακή.** — You come next Sunday.
- **Θα χαρώ πολύ να έρθετε.** — I would be very glad if you came.
- **Πάμε για καφέ την Τρίτη;** — Shall we go for a coffee on Tuesday?

**Making one invitation a month in the parish** is worth more for your Greek than any amount of study, because it converts acquaintances into people you talk to.

**Practice.** Say the eight invitations, five acceptances and six refusals aloud. Then accept three invitations and refuse two, with reasons and counter-offers. Then make one real invitation this week.
At someone's house:
Being a guest in a Greek house, which has rules — and they are rules of warmth rather than of formality.

**Arriving:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλώς σας βρήκα.** | the guest's greeting on arrival |
| **Καλώς ήρθατε!** / **Καλώς ορίσατε!** | the host's welcome |
| **Σας έφερα κάτι μικρό.** | I have brought you something small. |
| **Τι ωραίο σπίτι!** | What a lovely house! |
| **Να βγάλω τα παπούτσια;** | Shall I take my shoes off? |

**Καλώς ήρθατε and Καλώς σας βρήκα are a pair** — *welcome* and *I am glad to find you well* — and using the guest's half correctly is immediately noticed.

**Being fed, which is the main event:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Κάθισε, κάθισε!** | Sit down, sit down! |
| **Τι θα πιείς;** | What will you drink? |
| **Έφαγες; Θα φας κάτι.** | Have you eaten? You'll have something. |
| **Πάρε κι άλλο.** | Have some more. |
| **Δεν έφαγες τίποτα!** | You haven't eaten anything! |
| **Είναι πολύ νόστιμο, ευχαριστώ.** | It is very tasty, thank you. |
| **Φτάνει, ευχαριστώ, αλήθεια.** | That's enough, thank you, really. |
| **Χόρτασα.** | I am full. |

**Χόρτασα is the word that works** — *I am satisfied* — where **φτάνει** will be ignored. Expect to say it twice.

**The toast:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Στην υγειά μας!** | To our health! |
| **Γεια μας!** | Cheers! |
| **Στην υγειά σου!** | To your health! |
| **Και στα δικά σας!** | And to yours! — the reply at a celebration |

**Και στα δικά σας** is what you say back at a wedding or a baptism: *may your own come too*. It is the single most useful ritual phrase in Greek social life and it is said with a glass in hand.

**Leaving, which takes longer than you expect:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Πρέπει να πηγαίνουμε.** | We should be going. |
| **Μείνε κι άλλο!** | Stay longer! |
| **Ευχαριστούμε πολύ για όλα.** | Thank you very much for everything. |
| **Περάσαμε πολύ ωραία.** | We had a lovely time. |
| **Να έρθετε κι εσείς.** | You must come to us. |
| **Καλή σας νύχτα.** | Good night. |
| **Στο καλό.** | Go well. |

**The leaving sequence is three rounds**: you say you should go, they tell you to stay, you stay another twenty minutes, and then you leave. Leaving on the first attempt reads as abrupt.

**The house rules worth knowing:**

1. **Bring something.** Always, whatever was said.
2. **Accept what is offered**, at least once, including the thing you do not want.
3. **Compliment the food specifically** — **ο μουσακάς ήταν τέλειος**.
4. **The icon corner may be shown to you.** Looking at it with interest is the right response, and crossing yourself is yours to decide.
5. **Do not offer to wash up more than once**, and expect to be refused.
6. **Say goodbye to everyone individually**, including the children.

**Practice.** Say the arriving, eating, toasting and leaving phrases aloud. Then do the whole visit as a monologue: arrive, compliment, eat, refuse more food twice, toast, leave in three rounds. Then learn **Καλώς σας βρήκα** and **Και στα δικά σας** properly.
The parish hall:
The conversation this whole curriculum is for. Everything in stage 5, in the room where you will use it.

**What happens after the Liturgy**, in most Greek parishes: coffee, often food, and twenty minutes to an hour of talk in a hall or a courtyard. It is where the parish actually is, and it is a listening and speaking exercise that happens weekly whether you prepare or not.

**The opening, which is the same every week:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλή Κυριακή!** | the greeting of the day |
| **Χρόνια πολλά!** | if it is anyone's name day or a feast |
| **Τι κάνετε;** | to anyone older |
| **Ήταν ωραία η Λειτουργία.** | a safe and true opener |
| **Πολύς κόσμος σήμερα.** | a lot of people today |

**The ten things that will be said to you**, and having an answer to each is a week's preparation that lasts a year:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Από πού είσαι;** | Where are you from? |
| **Μιλάς ελληνικά!** | You speak Greek! |
| **Πόσο καιρό μαθαίνεις;** | How long have you been learning? |
| **Γιατί μαθαίνεις ελληνικά;** | Why are you learning Greek? |
| **Κατάλαβες τη Λειτουργία;** | Did you understand the Liturgy? |
| **Είσαι Ορθόδοξος;** | Are you Orthodox? |
| **Έχεις πάει στην Ελλάδα;** | Have you been to Greece? |
| **Έχεις οικογένεια;** | Are you married with children? |
| **Τι δουλειά κάνεις;** | What work do you do? |
| **Θα πιεις έναν καφέ;** | Will you have a coffee? |

**All ten are answerable with stage 2 to 5 grammar**, and the answers are worth writing out and saying aloud until they are automatic. That is not cheating: it is what the first six months of any conversation in a new language consists of.

**The questions you should ask**, because asking is what turns you from a curiosity into a participant:

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι εορτάζουμε σήμερα;** | What is today's feast? |
| **Πώς λέγεται αυτό στα ελληνικά;** | What is this called in Greek? |
| **Από πού είστε εσείς;** | Where are *you* from? |
| **Πόσο καιρό είστε εδώ;** | How long have you been here? |
| **Τι μαγειρεύετε;** | What are you cooking? |
| **Πότε είναι το επόμενο πανηγύρι;** | When is the next feast celebration? |
| **Μπορείτε να με βοηθήσετε με τα ελληνικά μου;** | Could you help me with my Greek? |

**That last one is the most productive sentence in this lesson.** Asked of the right person — often an older woman with time and opinions — it produces a weekly Greek lesson for free, delivered as conversation, which is exactly what you need and cannot buy.

**The things to say when you cannot follow:**

- **Συγγνώμη, δεν κατάλαβα. Πιο αργά, παρακαλώ.**
- **Μιλάτε πολύ γρήγορα για μένα!** — said with a smile, and always taken well.
- **Ακούω και μαθαίνω.** — I listen and I learn.

**And the one honest sentence that unlocks everything:** **Θέλω να μάθω ελληνικά για να μιλάω με εσάς.** — I want to learn Greek in order to talk to you. Say it once, to the right person, and your Greek will improve faster than any curriculum can manage.

**Practice.** Write and say aloud your answers to all ten questions. Then say the seven questions you will ask. Then this Sunday, ask one of them, for real, and stay for the answer.
Name days, feasts and what to say:
The Greek calendar of greetings, which is the most concentrated piece of useful social Greek there is — and the one that makes you part of a parish rather than a visitor to it.

**The name day — η γιορτή.** Everyone named after a saint celebrates on that saint's day, the day matters more than a birthday, and the greeting is **Χρόνια πολλά!**

| Name | Feast | |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Γιώργος / Γεωργία | 23 April | Άγιος Γεώργιος |
| Δημήτρης / Δήμητρα | 26 October | Άγιος Δημήτριος |
| Νικόλαος / Νικολέτα | 6 December | Άγιος Νικόλαος |
| Βασίλης / Βασιλική | 1 January | Άγιος Βασίλειος |
| Ιωάννης / Ιωάννα | 7 January | Άγιος Ιωάννης |
| Κωνσταντίνος / Ελένη | 21 May | SS Constantine and Helen |
| Μαρία / Παναγιώτης / Δέσποινα | 15 August | Κοίμηση της Θεοτόκου |
| Παρασκευή | 26 July | Αγία Παρασκευή |
| Ειρήνη | 5 May | Αγία Ειρήνη |
| Στέφανος | 27 December | Άγιος Στέφανος |
| Σοφία | 17 September | Αγία Σοφία |
| Ανδρέας | 30 November | Άγιος Ανδρέας |

**15 August is the biggest of them all** — the Dormition — and it is the name day of everyone called Μαρία, Παναγιώτης, Δέσποινα, Despina, Panayiota and a dozen variants. Half of Greece is greeted that day.

**What to say, and when:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Χρόνια πολλά!** | the universal feast greeting |
| **Να τα εκατοστήσεις!** | may you reach a hundred — to the person celebrating |
| **Και του χρόνου!** | and next year too |
| **Χρόνια πολλά και ευλογημένα.** | many and blessed years |
| **Να χαίρεσαι το όνομά σου.** | may you enjoy your name |
| **Περαστικά** | — no: that is for illness. Not this. |

**The great feasts and their greetings:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Καλά Χριστούγεννα** | Christmas |
| **Καλή Χρονιά** / **Ευτυχισμένος ο καινούργιος χρόνος** | New Year |
| **Καλή Σαρακοστή** | the start of Lent |
| **Καλή Ανάσταση** | Holy Week, before Pascha |
| **Χριστός Ανέστη! — Αληθώς Ανέστη!** | Pascha, and for forty days after |
| **Καλό Πάσχα** | Easter |
| **Χρόνια πολλά** | any other feast, including the parish's own |
| **Καλό μήνα** | on the first of the month |
| **Καλή εβδομάδα** | on a Monday |
| **Καλό καλοκαίρι / καλό χειμώνα** | at the turn of a season |

**Χριστός Ανέστη replaces hello entirely for forty days** — on the phone, in shops, everywhere — and the answer is always **Αληθώς Ανέστη**. Knowing that one exchange will carry you through the most important six weeks of the Greek year.

**The parish feast — το πανηγύρι.** Every church has a patron saint and that day is its festival: a Liturgy, often a procession, food, music and dancing. **Πότε είναι το πανηγύρι;** is a good question and attending is how you become known.

**What to do, as well as say:**

1. **Learn the name days of five people in your parish.** Write them down. Say **Χρόνια πολλά** on the day.
2. **Learn your own name's saint**, if it has one — the Greek equivalent may surprise you — and expect to be greeted on it.
3. **Take something small** to a name-day celebration: a sweet, flowers, or nothing if it is in the hall.

**Practice.** Learn the twelve name days above. Then find out the name days of five people you know and write them in your calendar. Then say all ten feast greetings aloud, and learn **Χριστός Ανέστη — Αληθώς Ανέστη** cold.
Reading: menus, notices and messages:
The real world's Greek, which is where the reading habit goes next — and it is all short, which makes it ideal.

**What to read now, in order of usefulness to you:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **The church notice board** | the week's services, the feast, the names, the times — weekly, repetitive, and exactly your vocabulary |
| **Menus** | section headings, dish names, and the abbreviations |
| **Shop signs and labels** | from stage 1, now with the compound words parsable |
| **Messages from Greek friends** | including Greeklish |
| **Parish Facebook and Instagram posts** | short, modern, idiomatic, and about things you know |
| **Street signs** | genitives, as stage 3 showed |
| **Public notices** | **Απαγορεύεται**, **Ενοικιάζεται**, **Λόγω έργων** |
| **Receipts** | the names of what you bought, which you already know |

**The notice board deserves the top place.** A typical one reads:

> **ΚΥΡΙΑΚΗ 26 ΟΚΤΩΒΡΙΟΥ — ΑΓΙΟΥ ΔΗΜΗΤΡΙΟΥ**
> Ὄρθρος 8:30 · Θεία Λειτουργία 9:30
> **ΤΕΤΑΡΤΗ** — Παράκλησις 6:00 μ.μ.
> **ΣΑΒΒΑΤΟ** — Ἑσπερινός 6:30 μ.μ.
> Τὸ Σάββατο θὰ τελεσθῇ μνημόσυνο ὑπὲρ ἀναπαύσεως…

**Note what that last line is.** It is not Modern Greek: **θὰ τελεσθῇ** is a learned passive and **ὑπὲρ ἀναπαύσεως** is a genitive with a preposition that modern Greek does not use that way, and the whole thing is in the old polytonic spelling. That is the register this curriculum deliberately skipped — and recognising it as *not your Greek* is itself the skill. The service names, days and times are readable; the formula is for the later curriculum.

**What to do with a notice you half-read:** take the four facts — day, feast, service, time — and ignore the rest. That is all anybody reads off it anyway.

**Messages, which are the most idiomatic Greek you will read:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Τι κάνεις; Όλα καλά;** | standard opener |
| **Είμαι στο δρόμο** | I am on my way |
| **Θα αργήσω 10'** | I will be ten minutes late |
| **Τα λέμε αύριο** | see you tomorrow |
| **ΟΚ, εντάξει** | fine |
| **Καλή σου μέρα 😊** | have a good day |
| **Σ' αγαπώ** | I love you — and note the elision |

**And the abbreviations**: **μ.μ.** (afternoon/evening, *post meridiem*), **π.μ.** (morning), **κ.λπ.** (etc.), **δηλ.** (that is), **π.χ.** (for example), **κ.** (Mr/Mrs), **αρ.** (number), **οδ.** (street).

**π.χ. and κ.λπ. are in every piece of written Greek** and worth recognising now.

**The intensive-reading exercise for this stage**: take one menu or one notice a week and read every single word, looking up what you do not know. Everything else should be extensive — read, get the four facts, move on.

**Practice.** Photograph or find your parish's notice board and read it aloud. Extract the four facts. Then read one Greek menu in full. Then read the last five messages a Greek friend sent you, if you have one, and work out any Greeklish.
Listening: the shop, the hall and the ph:
Three listening situations in order of difficulty, with what to do in each — because by now listening is the bottleneck.

**1. The shop or the café, which is the easiest.** Short, predictable, scripted, and with objects in front of you.

**What to expect**: **Τι θα πάρετε; · Κάτι άλλο; · Μετρητά ή κάρτα; · Θέλετε σακούλα; · Τίποτε άλλο;** and a number.

**The strategy**: know the script, listen for the number, and answer. If you miss something, **Συγγνώμη;** gets it repeated.

**2. The parish hall, which is medium and most valuable.** One person talking to you is manageable; several talking to each other is not, yet.

**The strategy**:

- **Stand near a conversation and listen without joining.** Ten minutes, deliberately, every week.
- **Count what you catch** — names, numbers, topics, whole sentences — and write the number down afterwards. It will go up over months.
- **When addressed, ask for slower rather than guessing.** **Πιο αργά, παρακαλώ** is always granted.
- **Expect to catch the subject but not the details**, which is the normal stage for a year or more.

**3. The phone, which is the hardest.** No face, compressed audio, and often an unfamiliar voice.

**The strategy**: have the sentences from the telephone lesson ready, say **Δεν σας ακούω καλά** early rather than late, and ask for a message in writing when it matters: **Μπορείτε να μου στείλετε μήνυμα;**

**And the structured listening that continues underneath:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Easy Greek, main tier** | with subtitles, then without |
| **The Easy Greek podcast** | the beginner one, with the transcript |
| **Helinika** | stories, slow |
| **Greek news, one headline at a time** | the ΕΡΤ bulletins are slow and clear |
| **Greek films and series with Greek subtitles** | and *Maestro in Blue* is the one everyone recommends |
| **The sermon** | weekly, free, and in the register you most want |

**Greek subtitles rather than English** is the rule once you can manage it: English subtitles turn listening into reading, and Greek ones make the sounds and the spellings line up.

**The four-pass method stays the same**: cold, with the text, cold again, then retell.

**What progress looks like**, so that you can recognise it: not *I understand more words*, but *the stream has broken into words*. That change is sudden, it happens somewhere in stages 5 to 7, and it comes from volume rather than from study.

**And the honest number**: at the end of stage 5 you might follow 30 to 50 per cent of a clear conversation addressed to you, and 10 to 20 per cent of two Greeks talking to each other. Those numbers feel discouraging written down and they are entirely normal.

**Practice.** This week: one shop exchange in Greek, ten deliberate minutes of listening in the hall with a count written down afterwards, and one Easy Greek clip with the four-pass method. Then do the same next week and compare the count.
Speaking: your first real conversations:
The lesson that matters most in this stage, and the one with the least content: you have to talk to people, and this is how to make that survivable.

**The problem, stated plainly.** You can now construct most sentences you need, slowly, with the grammar from stages 2 to 4 and the vocabulary from this one. What you cannot do is produce them at conversation speed, and the only cure is conversation.

**The four stages of getting there**, and they are worth doing in order:

**1. Talking to yourself, out loud, daily.** Narrate what you are doing. Describe your day in the past before bed. Argue with yourself. It is free, there is no embarrassment, and it builds the pathways that panic otherwise blocks.

**2. Scripted exchanges with strangers.** The shop, the bakery, the café. Short, low-stakes, and you know the script. Do one a week in Greek even if English is easier.

**3. The prepared conversation.** The ten parish-hall answers from earlier in this stage, said to a real person. Prepared is not cheating — it is how everybody starts.

**4. The unprepared conversation**, which is the goal and which will go badly for a while.

**The survival kit, which you should know cold before trying stage 4:**

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Συγγνώμη, δεν κατάλαβα.** | Sorry, I did not understand. |
| **Πιο αργά, παρακαλώ.** | More slowly, please. |
| **Πώς το λένε στα ελληνικά;** | How do you say it in Greek? |
| **Τι σημαίνει…;** | What does … mean? |
| **Μιλάω λίγα ελληνικά.** | I speak a little Greek. |
| **Μαθαίνω.** | I am learning. |
| **Μπορείτε να το γράψετε;** | Could you write it down? |
| **Μισό λεπτό…** | Just a moment… |
| **Πώς να το πω…** | How shall I put it… |
| **Δεν ξέρω τη λέξη, αλλά είναι σαν…** | I do not know the word, but it is like… |

**The last three are the fluency tools** — fillers that buy you time without switching to English. A learner who says **πώς να το πω…** and then finds the word sounds like someone speaking Greek; one who says *erm* in English sounds like someone failing to.

**The rules for your own speech at this stage:**

1. **Short sentences.** Two clauses at most.
2. **Simple tenses.** Present and aorist carry nearly everything.
3. **Do not translate from English in your head.** Say the simpler Greek thing you can actually say.
4. **Keep going through errors.** Correct nothing mid-sentence.
5. **Let them correct you**, and repeat the correction once, aloud.
6. **Do not switch to English** when it gets hard. That is the one habit that ends people's Greek: the moment English becomes the escape, the conversations all become English.

**Rule six is the important one.** In a diaspora parish nearly everyone speaks English, and the path of least resistance is permanent. You will have to be slightly tiresome about staying in Greek, and people will respect it.

**The one sentence that buys you the most goodwill**, from the parish-hall lesson and worth repeating here: **Θέλω να μάθω ελληνικά για να μιλάω με εσάς.** Say it once, early, to somebody who will remember it.

**Practice.** Today: ten minutes of narrating your own day out loud, in Greek. This week: one scripted exchange with a stranger, and one prepared conversation at church. Then the survival kit, aloud, until all ten come out without thinking.
Review: stage 5:
The end of stage 5. What should be true, and what stage 6 does.

**What should now be true — the vocabulary:**

- The house, its rooms and its contents, and how to say something is broken.
- Your daily routine in three tenses.
- Food, drink, the shops, the market, and the lenten vocabulary.
- A Greek menu, read and ordered from, with the **της ώρας / μαγειρευτά** distinction.
- Clothes, sizes, and what to wear to church.
- The body, what hurts, the doctor and the pharmacy.
- Money, the bank, the post, the phone, appointments.
- Travel by bus, boat and plane, and booking a room.
- Directions, asked and understood.
- The city, its services, and the acronyms of its bureaucracy.
- Work, school, and the family in full — including **κουμπάρος** and **νονός**.
- Feelings, opinions, agreement and disagreement.
- Small talk, the nine fillers, and the compliments you will receive.
- Invitations, being a guest, and the three-round goodbye.
- Name days, the feast greetings, and **Χριστός Ανέστη — Αληθώς Ανέστη**.

**What should now be true — the habits:**

- Ten words a day into the deck, chosen because you will use them.
- One real exchange in Greek a week, minimum.
- Narrating your own day out loud.
- A paragraph a day in writing.
- The notice board, menus and messages as reading.
- Deliberate listening in the hall, with a count.
- The survival kit automatic, and no switching to English.

**Where you are.** Roughly A2 going on B1: able to handle an ordinary day in Greek, hold a conversation about family, work, food and the weather, and take part in a parish hall without needing English. That is the level at which the language becomes self-sustaining — you can now learn Greek from Greeks rather than only from material.

**What stage 5 deliberately did not do.** Almost no new grammar: the perfect tenses, the conditional, the passive across the tenses and the participles are all still waiting. They were not needed to do any of the above, which is the argument for putting them after a stage of use rather than before it.

**What stage 6 does.** The rest of the verb: **έχω γράψει** and the perfect tenses, **είχα γράψει** and the pluperfect, **θα ήθελα** and the conditional — which you have been using as a phrase and will now understand — the passive in every tense, the participles, and reported speech. It is the stage that makes written Greek readable, because written Greek uses all of it.

**And the two tracks continue.** Spelling 2 and 3, Forms 2 and 3, which between them cover the verb endings you are about to need. If either track has fallen behind, this is the point to catch up — the next stage leans on both.

**Practice.** Go down both lists. Then have a ten-minute conversation with yourself covering five of the stage's situations. Then write down the three things from this stage you cannot yet say fluently, and make them next week's work.
